Learn about Finance Sikh and its educational approach to Indian personal finance.

Finance Sikh is an educational portal to help you understand the basics of personal finance.

Personal finance can be complicated. Terminology, regulations and features of various finance products can often confuse people. Finance Sikh aims to simplify those topics by breaking them down into straight forward topics with worked examples and helpful calculators.

This will help you learn more so that you understand what to think about.

## Topics

We have lots of educational content on Finance Sikh. We cover:

- Budgeting: How to manage your money each month.
- Saving: How to save for emergencies. What to think about when saving and types of saving.
- Investing: Mutual Funds, SIPs, Compounding, Risk and Long Term Investment Principles.
- Insurance: Term Insurance, Health Insurance, Policy Features, Exclusions and Waiting Periods.
- Taxes: Tax Concepts in India, Tax Regimes, Deductions and Common Tax Terms.
- Loans: EMIs, Repaying your loans, Credit Scores and Cost of Borrowing.
- Calculators: Explore Financial Calculations using clearly defined assumptions.

Note: The purpose of our content is to educate.

Your 2027 Financial Reset: 7 Money Checks to Make Before the New Year
Prepare your finances for 2027 with seven practical checks covering budgeting, emergency savings, insurance, debt, investments, tax planning and nominations in India.
Securities and Exchange Board of India
Association of Mutual Funds in India
Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India

When looking to reset your finances for the new year, you don’t need to go out and invest in new products. Instead, think about whether your money habits, savings, cover and goals match your lifestyle.

Take an hour out to look at your statements and policies and go through these 7 key checkpoints. Depending on your income, dependents, debt, job security and goals will determine what you prioritise.

## 1. Budgeting & Cashflow

This is about understanding where your money is going. Look at your most recent 2-3 months of bank and card statements. Categorise your expenses into essential, discretionary and non-essential. Essential expenses could be rent, food, utilities, transport, school fees, medication and minimum loan repayments.

List out your non-monthly expenses like your annual insurance premium, car servicing, school fees & festival travel. Work out how much you will spend in a year and divide this by 12. By setting aside this amount, you can plan for predictable bills.

Are you able to cover your essential expenses with your income? Are you saving for your annual expenses? Are you saving a realistic amount for your savings & discretionary? If your income varies each month, it’s best to budget using a conservative estimate.

## 2. Emergency Savings

An emergency fund can help provide some financial security when you have unexpected essential expenses or if you lose income. This can allow you to deal with a career change, urgent repairs or medical costs without having to sell long-term investments or borrow at a high cost.

As a guide, most people aim to save 3-6 months of essential expenses. However if you have one income earner, dependents or earn an unpredictable income with large EMIs, you may want to save a little more.

For example, if your essential monthly expenses are ₹35,000, you would save ₹1,05,000 for 3 months and ₹2,10,000 for 6 months. This is just an example. Work out your essential expenses including minimum loan repayments and any costs that you would still have to pay even if you cut back on your non-essential expenses.

It’s important to make sure you can easily access your money. Before deciding where to put your money, think about any rules or risks associated with withdrawing it. Don’t invest in shares or equity Mutual Funds as they can lose value when you need to withdraw. Make sure you know what [deposit protection](https://www.dicgc.org.in/) applies.

If you don’t have any savings, start with a small target and set up a manageable automatic payment after your payday. If you do use your emergency fund, think about how much you should be aiming to save and create a realistic plan.

Read our guide here on [Emergency Fund – How much to save?](/blog/emergency-fund/)

## 3. Health & Life Insurance

Just because you have insurance doesn’t mean you have sufficient cover.

With health insurance look at how much you are insured for, who is covered, any waiting periods, exclusions, co-payment clauses, maximum room rent and if you are covered for cashless or reimbursement. Read through all the policy wording and schedule. If you have employer provided insurance, think about what will happen if you leave your job.

With life insurance consider who depends on your income and what responsibilities you would have if your income stopped. Consider the policy term, how much you are insured for, exclusions, premium and nominee. Term insurance & health insurance are for different reasons.

Don’t cancel your policy just because it’s a new year. Think about whether you have the right cover, conditions and affordability. If you cancel your current cover and don’t have new cover in place you will have a gap. If you’re unsure ask your insurer to provide written confirmation.

## 4. High Interest Debt

Debt can impact how much you can save. List out all your loans/credit facilities, outstanding balance, interest rate, minimum payment, due date and any charges. This includes credit cards, personal loans, car loans etc.

Usually, paying the minimum payment on your credit card won’t clear the full balance. You may still be paying interest & charges depending on the terms. Look at your latest statement and agreement.

After you’ve paid your essential expenses and have a reasonable amount of cash in hand, look at the cost of borrowing. Paying off high interest debt can save you money in the future. However, look at any prepayment conditions and charges. Don’t use all your accessible savings as you may be likely to borrow again in an emergency.

Make sure you’re keeping up with the required payments. Any extra payments should go towards paying off the debt with the highest effective cost (taking fees and conditions into consideration). If you’re struggling to pay, get in touch with your lender as soon as possible.

## 5. Investments & Goals

Your investments should have a purpose. List out your main goals, when you might need the money and what investments you have for each goal. If you have a short term goal & retirement, you may need to approach this differently.

Look at your Mutual Funds, shares, deposits, provident fund & any other investments. Are you invested in a good mix for your goals and risk profile? Don’t invest too heavily in one company, sector or asset type as this could expose you to risks.

If you’re investing via SIPs, make sure they’re affordable and that they still fit the purpose. Don’t increase your SIP as the market has been performing well recently. Don’t stop your long-term investment as it’s dipped in the short term.

Look at the cost, documentation and asset allocation. Just because something has performed well in the past doesn’t mean it will in the future. Don’t make decisions purely based on social media recommendations or 1 year returns.

Use our [SIP Calculator](/calculators/sip-calculator/) to see how much your regular contributions could grow depending on the assumed return. If you’re considering taking withdrawals from your mutual fund corpus, use our [SWP Calculator](/calculators/swp-calculator/) to see how this may impact your balance. These are just examples.

## 6. Tax Records

Make sure you’re tax planning is in line with your income and tax year. Organise your salary statements, bank interest, investment details, insurance documentation, home loan statements & any other relevant documents.

If you’re a salaried employee, look at the different tax regimes available. Make sure you know what deductions/exemptions you have. The new tax regime is the default but eligible taxpayers may have the option to choose another tax regime. Don’t assume something will be beneficial just because it says it’s tax saving.

For 2026-27 look at the current guidance from the Income Tax Department and Income-tax Act, 2025. Tax forms, deadlines & eligibilty can change. If you have freelance income, capital gains, rental income or multiple sources of income make sure you’re keeping track of each category carefully. You may want to consider getting professional help.

Keep your documents organised for each tax year. Make sure your records match those on the official tax portal. Keep evidence of any eligible payments but don’t share any sensitive documents with unknown websites or agents.

Official guidance can be found here: [Income Tax Department – e-Filing](https://www.incometax.gov.in/iec/foportal/).

## 7. Nominees, Account Details & Important Documents

Without knowing where your family can find your accounts, your financial planning won’t be complete. Make sure you know who your nominees are for your bank, fixed deposits, Mutual Funds & insurance. Make sure the names and details are correct, especially if you’ve had a major change in your family.

The nominee may not be the ultimate owner of the asset depending on the asset and succession laws. Nomination can help an institution process a claim but it won’t replace estate planning or a valid will if required.

Make sure your address, mobile number, email, bank details & KYC details are correct with the relevant institutions. Keep a secure record of your institutions, policy numbers, account references & customer service. Never save any passwords, PINs, full card details or OTPs in a standard document.

Let a trusted family member know where your essential documents are.

## Simple 30 Day Financial Reset Plan

- **Week 1** – Understand your cashflow. Look at your statements and list out your essential monthly expenses. Know what annual expenses you have coming up.
- **Week 2** – Build your safety net. Work out how much you should be saving for your emergency fund. Look at your health & life insurance documents.
- **Week 3** – Deal with your obligations & investments. List out your debts. Look at the cost of interest. Look at your goals. See if your investments make sense.
- **Week 4** – Organisation. Organise your tax records. Check your nominee & KYC details. Secure your important documents.

Write down 3 things you’ll do and when you’ll review them. It’s better to have a short list that you can stick to than a long list that you’ll forget by February.

## Common Mistakes

Don’t fall into common traps such as investing in something just to save tax, investing your emergency fund in volatile assets, ignoring high cost debt, cancelling your insurance without new cover in place, chasing recent returns and leaving your nominee details out of date.

## FAQs

### What should I do financially before 2027?

Start by looking at your budget, emergency fund, insurance, debt, investments, tax records & nominee details. Focus on any urgent gaps.

### How much should I have in my emergency fund?

Most people aim to have between 3-6 months of essential expenses saved. If you earn an unpredictable income, have dependents or large repayments you may need to save more.

### Should I increase my SIP in 2027?

Only increase if you have the income, cashflow, emergency fund & any other obligations to allow you to. Make sure it still fits with your goals and risk profile. Don’t increase your contributions just because it’s a new year.

### Should I invest to save tax before the end of the year?

First look at the tax regimes available and make sure you’re eligible. Don’t invest in something just to try and get a deduction. Look at the official tax guidance or get advice from a qualified tax professional.

### How often should I review my finances?

Try to review your cashflow each month and have a more detailed review each year. If you’ve had a career change, new dependents, loan or income change, review.

## Final Thoughts

A Financial Reset isn’t about becoming a millionaire overnight or ticking off someone else’s checklist. It’s about knowing what you have coming in, going out, what you owe, what is protecting your household and what your savings are for.

Focus on fixing the most important gaps. Keep your records organised. If your life changes, review your decisions. Making small regular improvements can make your finances easier to manage throughout 2027.

Budgeting on an Indian Salary: Adapting the 50/30/20 Rule
Adapt the 50/30/20 budgeting idea to Indian households, including rent, family support, EMIs, annual bills and irregular monthly expenses on a salary.

The 50/30/20 rule can help to quickly allocate your post-tax income to three main areas. However, many Indians will not exactly match the percentage breakdown as rent, family support, school fees, health, travel and loan repayments can take up a lot of your income. The benefit of the rule is that you are ensuring that you are allocating every rupee towards something.

A typical breakdown would be to allocate 50% of your income towards your needs, 30% to your wants and 20% to savings or paying off extra debt. It is important to understand what falls in each category. For example, your home loan EMI may be a need whilst a subscription may be a want. Family support can be a must for some people whereas others may be able to give more flexibility to this category. Only once you have made your categories relevant to your situation will the rule be beneficial.

## Take your post-tax income

Always use your post-tax income (what you receive in your bank account after payroll deductions). If your post-tax income is Rs60,000 per month then you would allocate Rs30,000 to your needs, Rs18,000 to your wants and Rs12,000 to your savings or paying extra debt. This is just an example to demonstrate how the breakdown works.

If your income is variable due to incentives, overtime or commissions then it is best to create a budget based on your fixed income. Any variable income can be placed in a separate category until received.

## What should I assign to each category?

Needs – Essential expenses that you must pay to survive. This can include rent, food, electricity, basic travel, essential medication, minimum debt repayments and essential insurance. Wants – Non-essential expenses such as eating out, entertainment, upgrades, hobbies and non-essentials. Savings – Can include creating an emergency fund, long-term investments and paying extra debt.

Some things may fall into both categories. Whilst a mobile phone plan is essential for work, you may not need the most expensive plan. A car may be essential for travel but any extras/ upgrades can be a want. Family support may be a must so this shouldn’t be categorised as a want. Try to write why you are spending on each major thing.

## Example of an Indian salary

Let’s say your post-tax income is Rs60,000. You pay rent of Rs16,000, food and essentials of Rs7,000, utility and phone bills of Rs2,500, travel of Rs3,000, family support of Rs8,000 and EMI of Rs9,000. This totals up to Rs45,500. This means that you wouldn’t be able to follow the classic 50/30/20 rule as you would need to adjust your assumptions or categories. The correct answer here would be not to try to trick yourself into thinking your family support is a want or that you don’t need to pay your EMI.

You should first separate your must pay from your adjustable. Your rent could be fixed until the end of the lease, you could reduce your travel costs by travelling differently and subscriptions can easily be cancelled. You could also have a temporary breakdown of your percentages and review this when you get a raise, pay off your loan or move somewhere. A budget is there to help you make decisions.

## Budget for annual costs

Insurance, school fees, festival travel, car servicing and appliance replacements can cause a balanced monthly budget to go out of balance. They won’t necessarily be emergencies but you can still budget for them. Try to work out roughly how much you will pay yearly and divide by 12. For example if you have an annual bill of Rs24,000 then you should be setting aside Rs2,000 per month.

This will help to keep your cashflow in check. Otherwise you may feel that you have extra money for 11 months and then need to use your credit card for your big bill. You should also keep your emergency savings separate.

## Savings and Debt

The 20% can often be seen as savings but you may have many needs. You may need to create an emergency fund, save for an upcoming goal, invest for the long-term and pay off your expensive debt. This will depend on the interest rates, liquidity, risk and your situation. A budget rule will not determine which debt or investment you should prioritise.

If you have a minimum EMI payment then it is best to always allocate them to the same category. If your rule considers them to be needs then you can track your extra principal payments in the savings/debt section. Just ensure you aren’t double counting. Your spreadsheet should show what you are actually paying.

## What if my rent takes up half my salary?

Large city’s can mean that rent and travel can take up a lot of your income. If you are providing for your family then you may also find that you cannot fit the textbook breakdown. You could have a more realistic breakdown by increasing your needs and decreasing your wants. This is to show what you are spending your money on. You can always work on improving this gradually.

Some costs can only be negotiated when your contract ends. You may need to make a longer term decision such as moving closer to work or sharing a house. This will have its own trade offs but your budget should highlight these decisions.

## Monthly review

At the end of each month you should review what you were planning to spend and what you actually spent. Only look at the categories that had a significant impact on your total. If your food was higher due to family visiting then note this. If you keep going over your budget when shopping online then set a limit or think about putting a cooling off period in place.

A budget should be reviewed if there is a change in your life. Whether it be a new job, child, moving home, new loan or family support. You don’t need to review it weekly but having a quick monthly review can help you to see if you are drifting.

## Spreadsheet or Budget App

Many households will be fine using a spreadsheet. Create columns for date, amount, category and essential/want/variable. Some may prefer to use a budget app but ensure that you know the privacy settings and how it categorises your expenses. It should make your life easier.

Do not use your budget as an excuse to put off essential medical costs. If you are unable to afford your essentials then this may be an issue with your structure. Rather than focusing on your percentages you should look to understand your costs and get the right support.

## Conclusion

The 50/30/20 rule can be a helpful guide but many Indian household budgets will require a different breakdown. How Credit Scores Work in India and How to Improve One
Learn how Indian credit reports work, what affects scores, and how to check errors, raise disputes and build sustainable repayment habits without promises.

Your credit score is calculated using a credit scoring algorithm and information held by the credit information company. Lenders can use this alongside the credit report, income, obligations and other information to help them decide whether to lend you.

In India, credit information companies will hold reports based on information provided by credit institutions (credit institutions are members). Credit scoring algorithms can vary between companies as they are proprietary. As noted by the RBI, there is no standard scoring formula. Be wary of sites that claim to know exactly how much your score will go up by for doing one thing.

## What’s on a Credit Report?

A credit report can include lots of different pieces of information like your identity, credit accounts, repayment history, outstanding balances, credit limits and credit inquiries. This will vary depending on the report and the information provided by credit institutions. You should look at the names, addresses and account details provided. Whilst having the correct score is important, having the right account details and repayment status is also important.

Check the date of the report and the date the lender last reported. It can take some time for the latest payment to show on your report if they haven’t reported within their cycle. The RBI have given guidance on how often they should report. Check the current guidance. It doesn’t necessarily mean they’ve ignored your payment.

## Repayment History & Utilisation

Repayment history can impact how lenders see you. If you’re missing payments on a loan or card, this may be reported and can show on your report. However, if you’re making on time payments, this will help ensure your repayment history is accurate. However, there are other factors to consider such as other information, scoring algorithms and lender criteria.

Utilisation usually refers to how much of your available revolving credit you’re using. Having a high balance on your card may be seen differently than a low balance. There isn’t one specific percentage that will guarantee you a score. The balance and date can be important. Your card issuer may not have the same statement date as you. Don’t be tempted to use social media ‘magic numbers’.

## Credit Inquiries & Applications

If the lender are looking at your report as part of an application, they may show as an inquiry. If there are multiple applications within a short space of time, this can be seen differently than if you occasionally apply. If you’re checking your own report via an authorised consumer portal, this won’t count the same as multiple applications. Check with the credit information company for more details.

Don’t apply for multiple products to see which one will approve you. This can cause extra admin for the lender. If you’re rejected for a loan, check why, ensure there are no mistakes on your report and understand whether you could afford to borrow. Apply elsewhere.

## How to view your report

Go to the official website of the credit information company. You’ll need to verify your identity. As noted by the RBI, individuals can obtain one free full credit report (including score) per calendar year from the relevant credit information companies. [Verify current rules from the RBI regarding free full credit reports, how often they can be obtained, what channels they can be obtained from and how to escalate a complaint.]

Ensure all your accounts match what you have. Check there isn’t an outstanding loan, a late payment when you’ve paid on time, duplicate or not your account. Ensure your personal details are correct. Keep copies of statements, closure letters, payment confirmation and any other documents to help with disputes.

## Disputing Mistakes

If there seems to be a mistake on your account or repayment, use the official dispute process with the credit information company. If applicable, dispute with the lender providing the information too. Be specific about which account, what you’re disputing and what you want changed. Include any evidence to back up your dispute. Don’t send any sensitive documents through unofficial links.

Keep a note of your complaint reference. The bureau may need the reporting institution to investigate as they can’t always change the data. If you’re still having issues, check current RBI complaint process and how to escalate. Ensure you’re using the correct process.

## Good Habits

Set reminders or automatic payments so you don’t miss any due dates. Ensure you have enough funds in the account to make the payments. Check your statements to ensure there are no unexpected charges. Ensure any facilities you’ve closed are shown as such. Only borrow if you’ve considered whether you can fully afford to repay (including interest, fees and multiple EMIs).

Only close older accounts if you’ve considered the terms of the account and your needs. Don’t use one loan to pay off another without understanding the overall cost. You won’t improve your score by borrowing unnecessarily.

## Identity Theft

If there’s an unknown account or inquiry, this could be an indicator there’s an issue. Contact the lender and credit information company using official channels. Secure your bank and email accounts. Follow their guidance. Don’t ignore any suspicious entries just because the balance is low. Keep a note of your complaint. Check your report has been amended.

Be wary of services offering to remove accurate negative information or guarantee a certain number of points. Credit reports are governed by strict data processes. You can’t legally turn accurate history into a better score. They shouldn’t ask for your account passwords.

## Misconceptions

Having a high score doesn’t guarantee you’ll get approved for all loans. Having a low score doesn’t mean there’ll be one reason you’re being rejected. Scoring algorithms aren’t the same between companies and there isn’t a guaranteed number of points for doing one thing. Checking your report isn’t the same as applying for new credit. This will help reduce any unnecessary stress.

## Conclusion

Your credit score should be viewed alongside your full credit report and the lenders overall decision. Make sure you’re making your payments on time, ensure the information is correct and use official channels to amend any mistakes. Don’t borrow just to chase a number. It can take time for changes to happen and depend on the reporting and scoring process. Don’t promise a specific increase. Use current guidance from the RBI and credit information companies.

## What to do if you’re rejected

There can be many reasons for you being rejected. This can include your income, current obligations, how much you’re asking for, lender policies and the information on your credit report. Don’t assume it’s because of your score. Check why you were rejected, ensure there are no mistakes on your report and calculate whether you could afford to repay. Applying multiple times without understanding why can cause more inquiries.

If your account is showing as overdue due to a genuine mistake, use the official dispute process. If the information is correct, focus on getting your obligations up to date and ensuring you’re making sustainable payments. Don’t pay to guarantee it’ll be removed. Accurate data will be dealt with using the correct reporting and dispute process.

## Avoid falling for scams

Never give anyone claiming to fix your credit score your OTP, banking password or permission to access remotely. Ensure the website address and customer care details are correct. Be wary of guaranteed increases, fake government clearance certificates and advance fees to remove accurate history. Any legitimate dispute should be made through the credit information company and lender.

## Keep borrowing affordable

You can have a clean credit report but take on more debt than you can afford within your household budget. Before agreeing to a loan, calculate whether the EMI would fit within your rent, food, utilities, insurance, supporting family and repayments. Don’t forget to include irregular costs. Just because a lender is willing to give you a limit, doesn’t mean you can afford to borrow the full limit.

If you’re struggling to make repayments, contact the lender using official channels. Don’t ignore any notices. Ask what options you have available to you. Don’t take out a high cost loan to cover a regular EMI without calculating your new overall repayment. Your credit score is a record based metric. You should have a budget in place for your household.

## Checking your report

Once your dispute has been resolved, obtain a new report. Allow time for the relevant updates to be reported. The score won’t necessarily increase by a set amount. Even if there’s a mistake, your score can depend on other information and the proprietary algorithm. The aim of disputing is to have accurate data.

ELSS, PPF, and NPS Compared: Features, Lock-in, Risk, and Tax Treatment
Compare ELSS, PPF and NPS by structure, access, risk and tax treatment in India, with current rules flagged for verification and no product rankings clearly.

ELSS, PPF, and NPS often come up as a single unit in conversation. Whilst this isn’t an interchangeable product there are key differences between the products. ELSS is an equity based mutual fund scheme. PPF is a government small savings scheme with clear rules. NPS is a pension scheme with a regulated account and exit rules. There are key differences between the risk of the investments, limitations on access to the funds and the tax implications.

## Understanding the structure of the product

ELSS is an Equity Linked Savings Scheme (mutual fund). This means most of the fund will be invested in equities or equity related products. PPF will be invested in accordance with the small savings scheme rules. NPS will be invested in line with the pension scheme options. The NPS is designed to be a retirement scheme and has rules on how you can access the money.

The structure of the products is quite different. Mutual funds will see the NAV fluctuating. PPF will earn interest in accordance with the scheme rules. NPS will depend on the investment performance and charges. The reader shouldn’t see this as just variations of the same account.

## Liquidity

ELSS have lock-in periods in place for the investments made. Once the lock-in period has completed it can be redeemed in accordance with the scheme rules. The next SIP instalment will have a separate lock-in period. The exact details will need to be confirmed with the latest SEBI and scheme documents.

PPF has a long term period with specific rules around loans, partial withdrawals and maturity. Its not meant to be accessed daily. NPS has different rules around partial withdrawals and exits. Tier I is for retirement so has different partial withdrawal and exit rules. Tier II has different rules. [Verify the latest lock-in period for ELSS, withdrawal and extension rules for PPF and partial withdrawal and exit rules for NPS.]

Its not about which product can be accessed first. The household should consider when the money may be needed. Can it be withdrawn? What would be the value/tax implications? Emergency funds shouldn’t be locked away without having some fund that can be accessed.

## Investment Risk

ELSS has exposure to the equity market. The value of the investment can go up and down. Even though there is a lock-in period there is no assurance that the value won’t go down. PPF has different rules but there could be changes to the interest rate. This will be done via government notification. PPF has a long term period so can cause issues with liquidity. NPS has exposure to investment risk and has rules in place for when you can access the savings.

There are several factors to consider when looking at risk. This could be volatility, uncertainty, loss of buying power from inflation or not being able to access the funds when required. There may be little volatility with a product but not suitable for the goal due to the limited access. Some products could have more volatility but have a different role in a long term portfolio. The category of the product won’t give all the answers.

## Tax implications

Each product has different tax implications. This will depend on the tax year, product rules, contribution, eligibility and tax regime chosen. Older articles may mention rules from the Income-tax Act, 1961 but for tax years starting from 1 April 2026 tax will be in accordance with the Income-tax Act, 2025. Ensure you check the official tax portal and current law.

[Verify the current tax implications for the Tax Year 2026-27. This includes ELSS contributions and redemptions, PPF contributions, interest and maturity and NPS contributions, withdrawals and annuity income.]

If the product has tax deductions this will reduce your taxable income. It will not be risk free. Tax benefits may not be available in all tax regimes. Just because it has a tax free withdrawal in certain scenarios doesn’t mean it is tax free for all withdrawals.

## Costs and documents

For ELSS ensure you look at the scheme information document. Key Information Memorandum, expense ratio, portfolio details, riskometer and redemption rules. Costs will impact your experience. Different schemes will invest differently. Don’t choose a scheme based on the category having tax features.

For PPF ensure you check the latest scheme rules. The bank/post office will have instructions on how to operate. For NPS ensure you check the subscriber model. Investment options, charges, partial withdrawal rules and exit rules. Ensure you keep a record of statements and contributions.

## Example scenario

You may have three different goals. Money that could be needed for a medical emergency, money that is going to be invested for a long term wealth goal and money that is being saved for retirement. In this example the emergency fund will need to be easily accessible. The market linked mutual fund may have volatility. The retirement fund may have exit rules. The small savings scheme may have a long term period.

You could have different requirements at different stages. A long term product can be useful for saving but may not be suitable for a short term payment. The key thing to remember is that just because something has a tax label doesn’t mean it can be used for all financial goals.

## Common misconceptions

ELSS is not a guaranteed return product. You shouldn’t assume that the interest rate will stay the same for PPF. NPS is not a bank account that can be accessed. Tax implications for the contributions and withdrawals will be different. These reasons are why you should look at the main documents.

## Comparing historical figures

You shouldn’t compare historical figures from different time frames or with different risk profiles. A market linked fund’s return will be different to the notified small savings scheme. You should state why the return is different (volatility, changing rates, tax and time period). A comparison table should only include verified facts.

## Conclusion

Each product has a different legal structure, exposure, access and tax implications. Comparing these can be useful. Ensure you verify the current scheme rules and tax implications. Particularly the Tax Year 2026-27. Consider why the money may be needed. This article is purely for educational purposes and does not recommend investing in any option.

ELSS – Scheme information document, Key Information Memorandum, Portfolio details and costs. PPF – Latest government scheme documents and bank/post office instructions. Emergency Fund: How Much to Keep and Where to Keep It
Learn how essential expenses, dependants, job stability, EMIs and access needs shape an emergency fund, plus ways to rebuild it after a withdrawal event.

An emergency fund is money set aside for unpredictable, essential and urgent expenses. This is not for planned holidays, phone purchases or annual insurance. It can provide you with some breathing space if your income is interrupted or you have a large unexpected expense. Whilst emergency funds will not give you the best returns, it can provide access to your funds when you need it.

## How much should you save?

Depending on your situation, the amount you should save will be different. If you’re a salaried worker with a steady income and few dependents, compared to someone who works as a freelancer with unpredictable income or a family that has parents/children to support, the risk factors will be different. However, a good place to start is looking at your essential monthly costs. From here you can adjust the amount depending on your income stability, debt and responsibilities.

## Essential costs

Start by thinking about what essential costs you have. This could include rent/mortgage, basic food items, utility bills, transport to/from work, medication, insurance, school costs and the minimum loan payments. From here you can think about what you can reduce during a tough time. This doesn’t need to be an exact budget, just an estimate of what you’ll still need to pay even if your income drops suddenly.

Let’s say your essential costs are £35,000 per month. This means you’d need £105,000 for 3 months and £210,000 for 6 months. This is purely an example of how to calculate. Depending on whether your income is unstable, you have 1 main earner and dependents relying on your income or you might struggle to find a new job, you may want to save more. However, everyone’s situation will be different.

## Dependents, EMIs and job stability

You may have dependents which can affect your situation. If you have parents/children or another family member relying on your income, you may want to save more so you can still cover their essential costs. Medical costs can also be unpredictable. Although you may have some insurance to cover some costs, you may still have to pay some out of your own pocket.

It’s important to consider any loans you have. Usually, you’d still have to pay your home loan, car EMI or whatever you have to repay on a schedule. You’ll want to include the minimum you’d have to pay in your essential costs. Just because you’re unemployed or had an emergency, doesn’t mean your lender will allow you to pause paying.

Your job stability can affect how long you may be without an income. This depends on the industry you’re in, how many employers you have, the contracts you have, notice periods and how long it would take to find a similar job. If you’re self employed or a freelancer, you may also need to consider late invoicing or a customer who stops paying. An emergency fund is to help with uncertainty.

## Where to put the money?

Accessibility is key. If your emergency fund is in something that can fluctuate in value, you may lose money at the same time you need it. If you put your money into something with restrictions, penalties or long settlement times it could be inconvenient. The returns aren’t as important as knowing you can access it.

A savings account in a bank is a good choice. However, you may want to look into other deposit options. Make sure you know the terms of the institution, how quickly you can access your money and what protections are in place. In India we have DICGC which insures deposits, however this is only applicable if you meet the criteria and has limits. Please refer to the official explanation. Mutual funds, shares and other market related products aren’t deposits.

Some households may want to have some money easily accessible and some in a suitable account/deposit with clear terms. Keep it simple so you can access it in a stressful situation. Don’t spread your money across too many accounts that you won’t remember where it is.

## Costs of having the money in cash

Having the money in a low return account may mean you’re not getting as much as you would if you were investing for the long term. However, if you have to sell something that can fluctuate in value during a downturn due to an emergency, you may lose out or have to pay fees. If you have the money locked away, you may have to borrow at a high rate to cover an urgent expense.

Your emergency fund shouldn’t be ranked based on the job it does. Investing for the long term and saving for emergencies are two very different things. Trying to combine them can cause conflict when you’re in a tricky situation.

## Building up

Having a large target can be daunting if you haven’t saved much. Setting some goals can help you track your progress. Start with covering a small emergency, then work towards 1 months of essentials. Continue to build up to a larger amount based on your situation. These are just goals.

Setting up automatic transfers can help you save after receiving your salary. However, ensure you’re not causing any bills to bounce. Having it in a separate account or labelled clearly can help prevent you wanting to use it for planned purchases. Using windfalls, refunds or sporadic extra income can help you build it up. However your main plan shouldn’t rely on this.

## What is an emergency?

Sudden medical costs, essential home repairs, a loss of income or an urgent family trip could count. However, something like an annual insurance payment isn’t an unexpected cost as you knew it would come. This should go in your annual budget. Upgrading your phone is usually a planned purchase. Having clear definitions can help prevent you dipping into your fund.

Sometimes situations can be unclear. A car repair may be essential if you need it to get to work, however if you have another affordable option of transport it may not be. A family event may be important to you but not an emergency. You can set your own boundaries and review how much you’ve taken out after the situation has passed.

## Refilling

Using your fund isn’t a bad thing, that’s why it’s there! Once your emergency has passed, note down how much you used. Have an estimate of when you can realistically refill. If you’ve had a large withdrawal, you may want to cut back on your optional costs temporarily. However, you should still ensure you’re covering your essentials. Don’t try to refill straight away by borrowing at a high rate or investing all your remaining cash into a risky investment.

Sometimes you may realise that your target was too low. If you had to use most of your fund for an urgent bill, you may want to reassess how much you should have. Alternatively, if you keep using it for a planned purchase, you may want to set up a separate sinking fund in your budget.

## Common mistakes

A common mistake is to count your credit card limit as an emergency fund. Whilst borrowing can be useful in some situations, it isn’t cash you own. Another mistake is to put all of your emergency fund into an investment which can lose value. Lastly, you may set your target based on someone elses salary or social media rule. Your target should be based on your expenses and risk of your income.

Don’t forget to think about any irregular essential costs. Annual insurance, car servicing, school and medical costs can all be budgeted for separately. This way your emergency fund is there for any real surprises. You may want to reassess how much you have if you’ve moved house, changed jobs, added a new dependent, EMI or if there have been any big changes to your household costs.

## Conclusion

Having an emergency fund can give you some flexibility. How much you have should depend on your essential costs, dependents, debt payments and how reliable your income is. Where you save it should be accessible and you should understand the risk. An emergency fund isn’t there to give you the best returns, it’s there to help you. Build it up in manageable chunks and use it if you really are in an emergency. Once your household is stable, refill it.

## Separate emergency fund from planned purchases

A good way to help you keep your emergency fund is to have separate pots for your predictable irregular costs. This could include car insurance, annual payments, school admissions, festival travel and scheduled repairs. This means you won’t have to label them as emergencies when you receive the bill. It can also help you see if your monthly budget is actually balanced.

If you’re a cash user, keep it simple and just track how much you’ve taken out and put in. If you have multiple bank accounts, keep a secure note of what the account is for and how to access it. Don’t share your full details and don’t keep your passwords in an unsecured spreadsheet. It won’t help if you can’t access it safely.

## When to change your target

Having a new child, parent moving in, mortgage, changing from a salaried worker to self employed or having a long search for a job can change your risk. Instead of using your target from years ago, recalculate your essential costs. If your costs have decreased, for example you’ve paid off a loan or your dependents have become financially independent, you may want to reassess your fund. Don’t feel obliged to keep the number the same just because it felt like enough.

The aim is to have some resilience. Your target should be based on your real risk factors and be accessible.

EMI vs Prepayment: How Home-Loan Interest Works
Understand home-loan principal, interest, amortisation, fixed and floating rates, illustrative repayment schedules, and prepayment trade-offs and lender terms.

EMI’s are usually composed of interest plus principal repayments. The initial EMIs paid when you take out a fully amortising loan will be higher in interest due to the higher outstanding principal. As you start to pay down your loan the interest charged on the outstanding will decrease and more of your payment will make up your principal.

Depending on your loan agreement you may be charged a fixed, variable or other specified rate. There may be fees attached as well as a rule about when you can reset your rate. Your repayment dates and any rules around prepayment will also affect your cost. To ensure you know what you’re paying you should refer to your sanction letter and loan agreement.

Principal refers to the amount still owed on your loan, interest refers to the cost of borrowing the money. An EMI is an amount that is to be paid based on your loan terms. In a standard repayment schedule, your EMIs will cover your interest payment for the period and you’ll be paying down the amount owed (outstanding). This will depend on how your lender calculates it and any additional fees.

As an example, let’s look at an example loan of 30 Lakhs with a hypothetical 8% rate and 20 year term. This EMI will not reflect current market rates and will not include all possible fees. Your monthly rate may vary, this is due to the day count convention and when payments are made. Ensure you refer back to your terms.

Why your initial payments look different.

Your interest will be calculated based on the outstanding principal. Initially your interest will be high as your outstanding will be large. However, as you make multiple repayments your principal will reduce and therefore your interest will reduce if your rate remains fixed. This is known as an amortisation schedule.

You will get a repayment schedule showing how much of each repayment is going towards interest, principal and a new outstanding balance. You should review this when you take out your loan, when you reset your rate and if you make a prepayment. Your rate may change and therefore your EMIs, term or both may change depending on your agreement and any regulations. Ensure you check with your lender what changes they have made.

## Fixed and Variable Rates

With a fixed rate the rate will be fixed based on your contract. You should ensure you understand what “fixed” means and any rules around resetting or converting. With a variable rate your rate will be based on the benchmark, spread or other allowed terms. If rates increase your lender may increase your EMIs, term or both. If rates decrease it will depend on your terms and how it works.

A variable rate can mean there is some uncertainty around your repayments and total interest. A fixed rate may give you more certainty around your repayments, however there could be different rates or conversion terms. A fixed or variable rate does not necessarily mean one loan is cheaper overall. Check with your lender what the offer is, what the rules are around resetting and any fees. Also check how flexible your repayments are and how risky it is based on the rates.

## Prepayments

A prepayment is an extra payment towards your outstanding principal. Based on your lenders processes the prepayment may reduce your outstanding balance which could result in a shorter term, lower EMIs or other changes. Ask your lender how they will apply this amount and if there is anything you need to tell them to do what you want.

Paying down your principal sooner means that your interest will be less going forward. This will depend on when you pay, how much is outstanding, your interest rate, how much time is left and any fees/conditions. If your loan has been running for years, ensure you use the current balance and rate in your calculator.

Example:

If your outstanding balance was hypothetically 20 Lakhs and you paid an extra 1 Lakh towards your principal. Assuming your lender applies the full amount to your principal with no fees you’ll now have an outstanding of 19 Lakhs. Your future interest will be less based on your terms.

This is not necessarily true, as the 1 Lakh you’re paying is already yours. The benefit of paying is that it avoids interest being paid on the outstanding. However, if you need this money for medical bills, emergency savings or something else urgent you may want to consider this.

## Liquidity

Paying off your home loan can be satisfying as you’ll reduce your outstanding balance but you’ll have less liquid funds. Consider your emergency savings, upcoming bills, other debts, insurance requirements and how liquid your income is. You may not be able to get this money back easily unless you apply for further borrowing. How much liquidity you have will depend on your situation.

## Opportunity Cost

By paying off your loan you’re losing the opportunity to use this money for something else. While you may get a guaranteed reduction in interest based on your contract, there may be uncertainty around how much you could get back from investing. This may be taxed and there may be risk involved. This article will not advise what is best for you.

## Lenders Terms and Fees

When considering health insurance for your parents over the age of 60 it is important to consider all aspects of the policy. There can be waiting periods, co-payments, room limits, disease sub-limits, exclusions and pre-existing conditions clauses. These factors can affect how much you will pay out of your own pocket. Even though the policy seems cheap, it can be expensive.

## Consider

Start by thinking about what types of medical treatment you may require. What cover already do you have? What treatment are they currently undergoing and what is the financial capability of your family? Not everyone will be accepted onto the same policy at the same rate due to underwriting, medical history, geographical location, product design and insurance company guidelines. The official proposal and policy documents will dictate what is offered.

Who will be managing the administration? Older policy holders may feel more comfortable having their child or trusted relative helping them complete online tasks. However, you should ensure that they have the policy holder’s permission. You should also know how authorisation works. Ensure you have all policy numbers, customer services details and key documents so that you have them available during a hospital stay.

## Waiting Periods & Pre-existing Conditions

Waiting periods mean that you will not be covered for certain claims/conditions. Different products will offer different waiting periods, such as general waiting periods, waiting periods for certain diseases/procedures and waiting periods for pre-existing diseases. Ensure you know exactly what is covered and for how long by referring to your policy schedule and policy wording.

Ensure you accurately declare any medical history. Even if a condition is being managed with medication or hasn’t caused a recent hospitalisation, you shouldn’t assume it is irrelevant. If it is a question on the application form be sure to fully answer it to avoid any arguments. Ask the insurance company how they will manage the condition and keep a copy of their written reply.

## Co-pay

Co-pay means that you will pay a certain percentage of the eligible claim. This can vary between different policies. If there is a co-pay within your policy it is important to know whether it is a general co-pay, age band, certain hospitals and/or certain situations. Don’t assume based on the sales brochure.

This example is for illustrative purposes only. If a policy has a 20% co-pay on a claim of ₹1,00,000 it would mean you would pay ₹20,000 of the claim. This figure doesn’t take into consideration any deductibles, exclusions or sub-limits. This is purely an example. Real claims will depend on the policy and how the insurance company decide to manage the eligible costs.

## Room Limits & Sub-limits

Some policies will have a limit on what room you can claim for. If you choose a room that exceeds the limit outlined in your policy wording, you should know how this will affect your claim. Some policies will reduce any costs proportionally. How this is managed can vary so ask the insurance company how this will affect your claim. Keep a copy of their written response.

Sub-limits can apply to various treatments, procedures or costs. Some policies will have a limit on how much they will pay for a certain treatment. Even if your sum insured is higher than this amount, they will only pay up to the stated amount. Be sure to carefully review the detailed schedule.

## Pre-existing Conditions, Renewals & Premiums

Your parent may suffer from Diabetes, Hypertension or another condition that needs to be managed. Depending on what you declare, how they are underwritten, what the policy states and the regulations, you won’t know what will happen. This can’t be determined in a general article. Be sure to check the current IRDAI regulations and policy wording.

It is important to know how your policy will renew. This is to ensure you have cover. Find out how the premium is charged, when it needs to be paid, the grace period and what will happen if you don’t renew. Premiums can vary depending on the policy and regulations. Don’t assume that if you are quoted a price for age 61 you will pay the same price throughout the rest of your life. Policies can have various exclusions. Ensure you know what is excluded. Some policies will not cover consumables, non-medical items, outpatient, domiciliary, ambulance charges or certain procedures. The exact exclusions will vary. Don’t assume that because it says comprehensive cover it will cover everything.

Cashless can vary depending on the insurance company/authorised claims administrators and policy wording. It is important to know what you will have to pay for. You may have to pay for anything that isn’t approved. Keep a copy of your discharge summaries, prescriptions, bills, investigations and correspondence. Refer to the insurance company’s current list of documents they will require and deadlines.

Consider how much you are likely to be able to afford to pay for the premium. Choosing a policy that will be expensive to pay for can cause the policy to lapse when it is most valuable. Consider the whole package including premium, co-pay, room limits, sub-limits, exclusions, waiting periods and claims process.

Keep a copy of the written response from the insurance company.

Hospitals can vary in whether they are in the network. Ensure you know what the current status is. Have a realistic budget for any costs that may not be claimable. Insurance can help move some of the risk but not all costs will be covered and there may be issues when claiming.

Waiting periods, co-pay, room limits, exclusions and renewal can all have a big impact on what you pay. Ensure you review the official policy documents, check current IRDAI regulations and that the premium is something you can afford. This guide is for educational purposes only and is a checklist.

## Planning for a planned hospital stay

Review the pre-approval process from your insurance company and contact the official claims channel. Find out what documents will be required. Ensure you know what the current status of the hospital is. Just because they are in the network doesn’t mean you will get cashless approval. The insurance company will still use the policy wording and will review your request. Have a back-up plan in case you have to pay for anything.

In the event of an emergency you may not have time to review all the clauses. However, if you have the policy schedule, customer services number and ID documents to hand this can save you unnecessary delays. Ensure your trusted relative knows where they can find the documents. Keep a copy of your itemised bills, prescriptions, investigations and discharge summary once you have left the hospital.

## Renewal

Before you renew your policy ensure you understand what your sum insured, exclusions, co-pay and room cover are. If the insurance company offer you the option to change, migrate or port, ensure you know what the conditions are. How will continuity be managed? Don’t let your policy lapse whilst you are considering your options. The consequences can vary depending on the policy and regulations. A new application may be underwritten differently.

## Coordination with family

Ensure whoever is helping you with the claim knows who they can talk to and how consent will be obtained. Keep copies of your pre-approval requests, discharge documents, prescriptions, diagnostics and itemised invoices. If the hospital ask for an upfront payment ask what is an estimate and what has been approved. Approval can vary depending on the final bill and policy wording. Don’t assume that you will be paid for everything.

Once you have left the hospital compare the settlement statement to your bill. Ask the insurance company what clause has been used to reduce your claim. If your claim has been declined/partially approved use the grievance process. Keep a copy of their response. Refer to current official guidance from IRDAI on escalation and timescales. Don’t refer to an old forum answer.

## Network

Even though it is convenient to have a local network hospital, don’t forget to check room limits, treatment sub-limits, exclusions and co-pay. Hospitals can change their network status. Ensure you know what the current status is and have a realistic way to pay for any costs that aren’t covered. The aim is to not rely on one aspect of marketing and forget about the other limitations in the contract.

# How To Improve Your CIBIL Score In India In 10 Steps

A poor CIBIL score can affect your ability to borrow. This can be anything from credit cards to personal loans and mortgages. However, your CIBIL score isn’t set in stone and you can improve it over time by being responsible with your borrowing.

There isn’t a quick way to Improve Your score. Instead, learn what’s on your report, what the problem areas are and work on improving your habits. This guide will give you some realistic ways to Improve Your CIBIL score in India. It won’t guarantee you’ll get approved for a loan and you shouldn’t take any personal credit advice.

## What Is A CIBIL Score?

A CIBIL score is a 3 digit score which summarises your credit history. This is based on your Credit Information Report (CIR). It will generally range between 300 and 900. Lenders can use this alongside your income, existing EMIs and their own lending criteria.

The report will show information about your credit accounts including any loans or credit cards. However, it won’t include any savings, fixed deposits or investments. A high score can mean you’re better with your credit but doesn’t guarantee you’ll get approved for a loan.

## What Is A Good CIBIL Score?

Scores of 700+ are generally considered a good score according to CIBIL. Lenders will have their own criteria for what they consider a good score and this can vary depending on the product and applicant. A score closer to 900 can help boost your profile.

However, if you have a score of below 700, then it’s a good idea to look at your report before applying again. You may have missed payments, high credit card balances, too many applications, a short credit history or errors.

## 10 Ways To Improve Your CIBIL Score

### 1. Pay All EMIs And Credit Card Bills On Time

Your payment history is an important part of your credit profile. If you don’t pay on time, lenders may see you as a higher risk. Try setting reminders a few days before your due dates. If you’re using auto debit, make sure you’ve got enough money in your account linked. You can also check that your payment went through.

Wherever possible try to pay the full amount on your credit card. Whilst paying the minimum can prevent you from having a missed payment, the balance can accrue interest.

### 2. Keep Credit Card Utilisation Low

Credit utilisation shows how much of your available limit you’re using. For example if you have a credit card with a limit of ₹1,00,000 and your balance is ₹70,000 then you’re using 70% of your available limit. High utilisation can suggest you’re reliant on your credit.

Try to keep your balances well below your limit. It’s commonly suggested to keep it under 30% however this isn’t a guaranteed CIBIL score. If you can, try to pay some of your balance before your statement date. Don’t overspend as your limit is increased.

### 3. Don’t Apply for Too Many Loans or Cards

When you apply for credit with a lender, they may perform a hard search. If you’re applying for multiple credits in a short space of time, you’ll have multiple searches.

Before applying compare the eligibility, costs and terms of your loan. Only use eligibility tools if you know whether this will be a soft or hard search. Only apply if you really need it.

### 4. Check Your CIBIL Report Regularly

Your report will show whether you have any overdue amounts, unknown accounts, incorrect information and searches. CIBIL will give you one free CIBIL Score and Report per year through the official site.

Check that your report shows any closed loans are correct, that the balances look correct and that payments are being recorded correctly. Keep any receipts, statements and loan closure letters. Start here to get your [free CIBIL score and report](https://www.cibil.com/freecibilscore).

### 5. Dispute Any Errors

Your report may show incorrect overdue amounts, loans you didn’t take out, duplicate accounts or payments which haven’t been updated. Dispute this with CIBIL and get in touch with the lender who provided the information.

The Public Provident Fund (PPF) is a small savings scheme that is backed by the Government. Unlike a bank savings account your money will be invested for a long period of time and will be subject to the rules of the scheme. It is also different to a market linked mutual fund as the PPF account follows the rules of the notified scheme and therefore the interest rate can vary dependent on declaration by the Government. When researching a PPF you should look at the difference between the interest rate and the rules of the scheme.

## PPF Structure & Eligibility

This account can be opened in the name of an eligible individual either via an authorised bank or post office. The rules state who can open the account, if there can be joint names on the account, how the account operates for minors and that you cannot open more than one account in the same name. You should look at the latest official documentation for the rules of the scheme. There may be additional steps required by the banks/post offices for you to complete to ensure you meet the requirements for opening the account such as confirming your identity, nominating and making deposits.

The PPF account is designed for long term savings. You will make deposits into the account and interest will be added using the interest calculation method from the scheme. As the timing of the deposits may affect the interest, do not assume that you can make deposits on any day of the year. The latest official guidance will tell you what the calculation method is and what the timing requirements are.

## Minimum and Maximum Deposits

The official documentation for the scheme will state what the minimum deposit per year is and the maximum amount that can be contributed to the account. This should be checked to ensure the correct information is known as these are facts and could change. If you are unable to meet the minimum deposit requirement the account could be affected and there may be a process to reactivate the account and/or charges applied based on the rules. Do not rely on information from an old blog or screenshot.

Your deposits should be planned to ensure they work with your cash flow and you are not needing to borrow or ignore any immediate payments. You can choose to make a monthly deposit, however the PPF scheme may allow different deposit patterns. The timing should take into consideration your salary dates, annual costs and how much cash you have available outside of the account. The PPF is not a substitute for emergency cash.

## Length of Investment & Extending the Account

The PPF is intended to be a long term investment however there are rules in place regarding extending the account. The maturity date will impact when you can access the funds and what options you have. The process for extending the account and how any additional contributions will be dealt with should be checked against the latest official rules. Do not assume all extension options will have the same impact.

When opening an account you should consider how long the funds will be tied up for and whether this works with your reasons for opening the account. If you need the money for a deposit on a house, a business cost or school fee before the maturity date then you may need to hold funds elsewhere. Whilst having a long investment period can encourage you to save for the future it can also have less flexibility. Ensure you know what the account will be used for before making large deposits into it.

## Interest Rate Declarations

The interest rates are declared by the Government for small savings schemes for specific periods of time. The interest rate shown on the official page is a declaration for the period and is not guaranteed to be the rate for the whole life of your new account. You can be misled if you calculate using the rate for 15 years as this is an example.

Using an online calculator you should check if the calculator assumes a fixed rate. If so then this is an example. More carefully, you should note what rate was used and when it was checked. Future declarations may vary. The actual balance in the account will be based on the rules and rates.

## Withdrawing & Loans

The PPF has specific rules for when partial withdrawals can be made, how much can be withdrawn and if there is an option for loans during a specific period. The account will need to be a certain age and meet the conditions of the scheme. It is not a regular savings account and you should not assume you can withdraw at any time you need to pay for something. You should check the latest rules with the official scheme and the institution.

Having restrictions on accessing your funds can be both a positive and a negative. If you have an irregular income, dependents or high medical exposure you may want to have a separate cash fund. Having your emergency cash tied up in a long term account can cause problems with timing.

## Tax Status

Historically the PPF has had tax benefits. However the tax status will depend on the law, tax year, your situation and the regime you are choosing. The Income-tax Act and rules can change so terms used in older articles may not be the same as now. Not all taxpayers will find it beneficial to get a tax deduction. Depending on the regime you may not be able to claim it or it may not be relevant. You should not make a contribution purely to get a tax tag on the account. You should always refer to the official Income Tax Department guidance.

## Drawbacks

The most obvious downside is the long investment period, however there are several others. The interest rate can change, the account can be restrictive and it isn’t as exposed to the market as an equity investment. Just because it is Government backed doesn’t mean it will be suitable for all purposes. When comparing to other savings you should look at the purpose and rules.

There can also be administration issues. Ensuring the details are up to date, deposits have been added to the account, keeping statements, knowing what your nominations are and ensuring any service is completed correctly. A small error when making deposits can cause problems when trying to access your funds at maturity/withdrawal. Keep records and use the official process with your institution.

## Common Misconceptions

The PPF is not a daily account. Do not assume the interest rate will stay the same for the whole investment period. Do not assume you will automatically be able to extend your account on your preferred terms. Do not assume the tax status will be the same as in an article before 2026. A long term account can be difficult to change once you have deposited your funds.

## Summary

The PPF is a long term small savings scheme with set rules on contributions, maturity and withdrawal. It may be suitable for some long term savings purposes however you should be aware of the lack of liquidity and varying interest rates. You should check the latest scheme documentation for rules, check what the conditions are for making deposits and withdrawing and check the tax status. This is an explanatory guide outlining what the account is like. Whether it is suitable for your household will depend on your circumstances.

## Administration for Long Term Account

As the account will run for a long period of time you may have moved house, changed your phone number, bank or family circumstances. Ensure your contact details are updated, check your nominations and store your account details securely. If you are moving your account between an authorised bank and post office you should follow the current official process and keep evidence of your request. Never give away your passwords, PIN or one time passwords to someone claiming to help you with an everyday update.

Before your account reaches maturity check what the official process is and what the deadline is for requesting an extension or withdrawal. Do not leave it until the last week to find out you need to fill in forms, sign and confirm your identity. The exact process can vary per institution so you should check the current written guidance.

## Consideration for Household

You should think about what your immediate cash needs are, other savings and any long term commitments. If you have a large balance in a locked account you may still struggle to pay for something unexpected if you don’t have an emergency cash fund. Some people may like having a structured long term account and intentionally keep some money separate for shorter term. Knowing what the purpose of the account is will make it clearer.

Don’t be confused by the Government backed scheme. This doesn’t mean you will get the same rate and rules in the future. The account will operate based on the legal terms and official declarations. You should double check these when making a big decision.

## Double Check Information

If you are seeing different info in your bank app, post office passbook and online calculator firstly check the dates and that all your deposits have been added. The projection may be using a fixed rate whereas your actual account will show the rate applicable for the periods. Check your transaction ledger and official interest rate declaration. If you still can’t understand why there is a difference you should contact your institution using their official process and keep your complaint reference.

You should be aware of the difference between the maximum deposit and maximum balance. If there is a maximum deposit per year based on the rules of the scheme this does not mean there is a maximum balance. The current official rules will tell you what the maximum is and what will happen if you exceed it. Do not assume based on what a calculator says or what someone else says.
