How Much Should You Invest Monthly to Reach a Goal? A Reverse SIP Guide
A guide to reverse SIP calculations, future-value assumptions, time horizons and return sensitivity, using illustrative rupee examples rather than forecasts.

A reverse SIP calculation takes a target goal and calculates what you would need to contribute regularly to achieve this. Essentially you’re calculating how much you’d need to contribute each month to achieve your chosen target amount, based on your assumptions. This is a very useful tool to help you plan how you will achieve your goal but is not a prediction. The accuracy of the calculation will depend on how well you know how long you’ll be contributing for, when you’ll be contributing and what rate of return you’re assuming.

This can be useful to make a big goal feel more tangible. By putting a number and date on your goal (e.g. future education costs, a future purchase you want to make or long term savings) you can understand what you’re aiming for. However, you may need to factor in inflation for your goal amount and increase your contribution depending on changes in your income. Using a calculator can also help you have a discussion around your assumptions.

## Know your goal

Start by writing down what the money is for and when you’ll need it. A goal such as ‘build wealth’ is too vague. You need to be specific with your goal. You could write ‘save an illustrative ₹8 lakh in 8 years’. This gives you something to work with but your target amount may not be exactly what you’ll need to pay in the future. If you’re saving for a future expense you may want to factor in that the price could go up.

## How much do you currently have?

If you currently have some savings then your total to build will be less than if you have nothing. However, don’t include emergency savings or money for another commitment. Your goal should reflect how much really can be allocated towards it.

## Maths behind the calculation

Most reverse SIP calculators use a future value calculation. This assumes you’re making regular monthly contributions, growing at a steady rate (converted to a monthly rate). This gives you an approximation of how much you’ll have. Most calculators will assume you’re contributing at the end of each month. This will slightly alter your answer.

Investment returns will not be a straight line. Investments linked to the market will fluctuate and your returns may be affected by charges and tax. Using a steady rate calculation helps you to see your assumptions and compare them. However, it won’t reflect every market scenario. Check how the calculator handles compounding, contribution dates, initial capital and charges.

## Example in rupees

Let’s say your goal is to have an illustrative ₹8,00,000 in 8 years. This calculator may ask you to try several rates of return. The higher the rate you assume the less you’ll need to contribute each month. These are just hypothetical numbers. The lower the rate you assume the higher you’ll need to contribute each month. This is purely maths and doesn’t mean you can pick a higher rate of return to make the monthly figure look good.

It’s best to run at least three scenarios. One with a conservative rate of return, one with a moderate rate (just to compare) and one with a higher rate of return to see how sensitive your goal is. All results should be noted as illustrative. If you’re only achieving your goal with the highest rate of return then your goal may be quite uncertain. Just because you’re contributing an amount that looks affordable doesn’t mean you’ll achieve your goal.

## Time

The longer you contribute for the more time your monthly contributions will have to build up and earn returns. This will often mean you’ll be able to achieve your goal with a lower monthly contribution. If you’re contributing for a shorter period of time you’ll generally need to contribute more as there will be fewer contributions and less compounding.

Check when your goal is. An 8 year goal is not the same as an 8 year and 6 month goal. If you’re contributing monthly the number of contributions and dates will affect how much you’ll need. Also check if your first contribution will be immediately or in one month. Don’t compare two calculators unless they have the same assumptions.

## Sensitivity

Having one rate of return can give you a false sense of security. Increasing the rate by a little may mean your contribution decreases a lot and looks good. However, you don’t get to choose what happens in the market. Equity values could decrease, debt investments could have credit or interest rate risk and different funds will behave differently. Inflation will also affect how much you’ll have.

A useful way of seeing how sensitive your goal is is to change one assumption at a time. Start by keeping your goal and time frame the same but trying different rates of return. Next keep your rate the same but shorten the time frame. Finally think about increasing your goal as the cost may increase. This isn’t to give you a perfect prediction but to show you what your goal depends on the most.

## Not a fixed contribution

Most basic reverse SIP calculations assume you’ll be contributing the same amount each month. In reality your salary could increase, decrease or be interrupted. Some households may be able to increase their contributions each year whereas others may need to decrease during times of unemployment or family expenditure. If you’re planning to increase your contributions in steps you’ll need to do a different calculation. The increases should be realistic.

If you’re reviewing your plan yearly you should check how much you’re contributing. If you’re missing out on contributions this can impact how much you have at the end, especially if it’s early on and you’ve lost out on compounding. Adding extra later may help but it will depend on how much you’re adding, when and what your actual returns are. Don’t use a calculator as a replacement for checking your plan against your cash flow.

## Inflation

A goal of ₹8 lakh in the future may seem like a lot now but after several years of inflation it may not be as much. If your goal is related to education, healthcare or housing make sure you’re estimating how much it will cost in the future. When making assumptions around inflation make sure to label them as assumptions and review them using credible data when updating this article.

Inflation is not the same as investment returns. A nominal return is how much your investment has increased in rupees. A real return takes into consideration how much your purchasing power has changed after inflation. Whilst your calculator may be mathematically accurate you may not have enough to buy the products/services you wanted. Your goal should reflect what it will be used for in the real world.

## Understanding your answer

Your answer will give you a rough idea of how much you’ll need to contribute each month. Think about whether this fits with your essential expenditure, debt repayments and cash buffer. If not you should consider changing your goal, time frame or contributions. Don’t assume you’ll get a better return by being an aggressive investor. Some goals can be delayed or come from multiple sources whereas others will be on a fixed date. You’ll need to make practical decisions based on your goal and household.

## The investment

A calculator won’t tell you what mutual fund or investment to use. Your risk, liquidity, charges, tax and when you need the money will all impact whether it’s suitable for your goal. Just because you’re contributing for a longer period of time doesn’t mean all high risk investments will be suitable. You may need to go for something with less volatility but it may not keep up with inflation.

## Common mistakes

Don’t mix up annual percentage returns and monthly rates. Make sure to check how the calculator converts these. Don’t forget to include any initial lump sum. Don’t assume you’ll definitely have the amount shown. Don’t forget to include costs.

Don’t be tempted to use a calculator that gives a very specific figure in rupees. Make sure you understand what the inputs are.

Setting a goal based on an unrealistic contribution amount. It may be more honest to start with a lower recurring contribution that fits within your household budget. If you have a large contribution amount but pause it after a few months this may not be the best approach. If your income, family commitments, cost of goal or date changes make sure to review your plan.

## Conclusion

Reverse SIP planning will help you see how much you may need to contribute to achieve your future goal based on your assumptions. It’s useful to understand how your goal amount, time frame, contribution and sensitivity to returns will impact your goal. It’s not a guarantee and your real investment journey won’t be as straightforward as a formula. Try several scenarios, factor in inflation and costs and make sure you understand the assumptions made by the calculator.

## Goal worksheet

Start by writing down your goal amount, when you’ll need the money, how much you’ve already set aside and how much you can contribute each month without borrowing. Note down the assumptions you made around your returns and when the calculator assumes you’ll be making deposits. Write down your inflation assumptions separately and if you plan to increase your contributions each year. This will help you see why you may be getting a disappointing result based on your goal, time frame or contribution.

If your goal changes make sure to review your worksheet. If your course fee has increased you may need to update your goal. If your salary has increased you may be able to increase your contributions. If your income is uncertain you may need to reduce your contribution schedule. All changes should be made honestly.

## Buffer

If your goal is calculated to the last rupee you’ll have no buffer for returns not being as high as assumed, missing out on contributions or the cost increasing unexpectedly. This can be done by increasing your goal amount or reducing your return assumption. How much of a buffer you should have will depend on your goal and household. There is no one percentage that will guarantee your investment.

The most useful thing a calculator can do is show you how fragile your goal is. If your goal looks unachievable with a small change in your assumptions this is useful to know early on.

SEBI Makes Direct Mutual Fund Plans Default: What Investors in India Need to Know
From 1st November 2026, Direct Mutual Fund plans are the default option on AMCs' digital platforms. Learn what this means for investors in India.

As of 1st November 2026, Direct Mutual Fund plans are now the default option available on AMCs' digital platforms. If you wish to invest in Regular Mutual Fund plans, you should be made aware of the higher expense ratios.

This doesn't mean they've been banned, or that you'll get better returns, it simply means that if you're investing on an AMC's digital platform you'll see the Direct Mutual Fund option as the default. Here's what you need to know as an investor.

## What's changed from 1st November?

The change was announced by SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey on 28th October. This means if you're investing via a digital platform of an AMC (their website or app) you'll see the Direct Plan as the default. You'll still be able to invest in a Regular Plan, however you will need to be made aware of the higher expense ratio.

This announcement is regarding the digital platforms of AMCs. Not all banks, distributor apps or 3rd party platforms will need to change. However, do take note of which plan you're viewing.

## Direct Plan vs Regular Plan

Most Mutual Fund schemes will have both Direct and Regular options. These are both part of the same scheme, so will have the same underlying portfolio and fund manager. The key difference between them is how they're distributed.

### Direct Plan

A Direct Plan is bought directly from the Mutual Fund House. As you're not paying any distributor fees this will normally have a lower expense ratio than the Regular Plan. This could be the right option for those who can understand the risk in the fund, pick the right schemes for them and keep track of their investments. However, they may also pay for professional advice separately.

### Regular Plan

A Regular Plan is bought via a distributor/intermediary. As there are distribution fees involved this will generally have a higher expense ratio. This isn't necessarily a bad thing. Some investors like having support with their transactions, understanding the products and having support during volatile times. Consider if you're getting value for money.

## What is the expense ratio?

The expense ratio is the amount of money charged regularly to manage your Mutual Fund scheme. This gets added to the Net Asset Value (NAV) of your scheme.

The lower the expense ratio the less of the scheme you'll have to pay for. Over a long period this could mean you have more money invested into your scheme due to lower costs. If you're earning the same pre-expense returns from both versions of the fund, then the Direct Plan will generally have a higher net return due to the low expense ratio.

This doesn't guarantee a better investment. Both schemes will have the same risks. However, the costs won't help you avoid any drops in the market, poor asset allocation or wrong fund.

## Is Direct always better?

No. Whilst having a lower expense ratio is an important factor to consider,

A Direct Plan may be suitable if you understand what fund category you're investing in, know what the risk is, what the objective is, what the time frame is and what the asset allocation is. Also if you're happy to review your investments.

A Regular Plan may be helpful if you need support with picking your funds. Make sure you understand how your distributor is being paid and what services they're providing. Just because they're charging a fee doesn't mean they'll give you good advice or better returns. Consider how much you can manage yourself and if you need the support.

## What if I'm already invested in a Regular Plan?

You won't automatically be switched to a Direct Plan. Regular Plans haven't been removed. Don't feel the need to switch.

However, switching to a Direct Plan is usually seen as a switch. This means you'll have to redeem your units and purchase them again. This could mean you pay capital gain tax. You may also pay an exit load depending on your scheme and how long you've held the units.

**Before switching consider:**

- **What is the expense ratio?** Compare the expense ratios of the Direct Plan and Regular Plan. This is for the exact same scheme.
- **Will I pay capital gains?** Work out if switching will cause you to pay capital gain.
- **Will I pay an exit load?** Check what the exit load is for your scheme and how long you've held your units.
- **Am I getting value for money?** Do you currently get any useful support from your distributor?
- **Is this the right scheme for me?** Make sure the scheme and asset allocation suits your financial goals.

If you have a large portfolio or complex tax situation you may want to speak to a qualified tax professional or appropriately registered investment adviser.

## Things to check before investing

**Make sure:**

- You're investing in the correct plan type.
- You're investing in the correct scheme. Don't invest in two similar schemes.
- Compare the expense ratios. Check the latest Total Expense Ratio (TER) for your scheme.
- Understand the risk. Read through the scheme information and understand what the risk level is.
- Consider your goals. Make sure the fund suits your time frame and asset allocation.
- Know who's advising you. Do you get any services from your distributor? Are you getting registered investment advice? Or just access to transactions?
- Keep a record. Keep a copy of your confirmation and periodically check your consolidated portfolio statement.

## What does this mean for the Mutual Fund industry in India?

This puts more of a focus on showing the costs of your investment clearly. Having a default option can impact what you choose, especially if you're new to investing in Mutual Funds and didn't know there were two options. This means people who want to invest without using a distributor may not accidentally choose an option with a higher cost. It may also put more focus on asking your distributor what services they provide and how they charge.

However, just because it's easier to access doesn't mean you'll understand how to invest. You will still need to understand the risks, diversification, costs, time frames and difference between execution and personal advice. Distributors may need to show the value they provide and AMCs should ensure they're providing clear disclosures.

## FAQs

1. **Are Regular Mutual Fund Plans no longer available from November 2026?**  
   No. They're still available. However, Direct Mutual Fund Plans will now be the default option on AMCs' digital platforms. You'll need to be made aware of the higher expense ratios if you choose to invest in Regular Mutual Fund Plans.

2. **Will my current Regular plan automatically be switched to a Direct plan?**  
   No. You won't be automatically switched. Take a look at your current holdings and consider the tax and exit load implications.

3. **Do Direct and Regular Plans invest in different stocks?**  
   No. Both the Direct and Regular options will have the same underlying portfolio and fund manager. The main difference is how they're distributed and the expense ratios.

4. **Is a Direct Plan suitable for everyone?**  
   Not necessarily. It may be suitable for those who can pick and monitor their funds. However, if you need regular support you may appreciate the support from your distributor. Just make sure you understand the cost.

5. **Where can I find the expense ratio for a Mutual Fund?**  
   Check the scheme disclosures from the AMC. Also check the Total Expense Ratio information from AMFI. Compare the Direct and Regular options for the same scheme. Check the latest disclosure.

## Conclusion

The change to having Direct Mutual Fund Plans as the default option is a reminder that costs are important. From 1st November 2026 you're more likely to see the Direct Plans as the default option if you're investing on an AMCs' digital platforms. However, Regular Plans are still available with a higher expense ratio disclosure.

Don't just switch or invest because it's the default option. Make sure you understand the costs, what support you're getting, what the risk is in the fund and if you can manage your investment. An appropriate investment decision is one that suits your financial goals and behaviours.

Most Mutual Fund schemes will have both Direct and Regular options. These are both part of the same scheme, so will have the same underlying portfolio and fund manager. The key difference between them is how they’re distributed.

Direct Plan

A Direct Plan is bought directly from the Mutual Fund House. As you’re not paying any distributor fees this will normally have a lower expense ratio than the Regular Plan. This could be the right option for those who can understand the risk in the fund, pick the right schemes for them and keep track of their investments. However, they may also pay for professional advice separately.

Regular Plan

A Regular Plan is bought via a distributor/intermediary. As there are distribution fees involved this will generally have a higher expense ratio. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing. Some investors like having support with their transactions, understanding the products and having support during volatile times. Consider if you’re getting value for money.

What is the expense ratio?

The expense ratio is the amount of money charged regularly to manage your Mutual Fund scheme. This gets added to the Net Asset Value (NAV) of your scheme.

The lower the expense ratio the less of the scheme you’ll have to pay for. Over a long period this could mean you have more money invested into your scheme due to lower costs. If you’re earning the same pre-expense returns from both versions of the fund, then the Direct Plan will generally have a higher net return due to the low expense ratio.

This doesn’t guarantee a better investment. Both schemes will have the same risks. However, the costs won’t help you avoid any drops in the market, poor asset allocation or wrong fund.

Is Direct always better?

No. Whilst having a lower expense ratio is an important factor to consider,

A Direct Plan may be suitable if you understand what fund category you’re investing in, know what the risk is, what the objective is, what the time frame is and what the asset allocation is. Also if you’re happy to review your investments.

A Regular Plan may be helpful if you need support with picking your funds. Make sure you understand how your distributor is being paid and what services they’re providing. Just because they’re charging a fee doesn’t mean they’ll give you good advice or better returns. Consider how much you can manage yourself and if you need the support.

What if I’m already invested in a Regular Plan?

You won’t automatically be switched to a Direct Plan. Regular Plans haven’t been removed. Don’t feel the need to switch.

However, switching to a Direct Plan is usually seen as a switch. This means you’ll have to redeem your units and purchase them again. This could mean you pay capital gain tax. You may also pay an exit load depending on your scheme and how long you’ve held the units.

Before switching consider:

  • What is the expense ratio? Compare the expense ratios of the Direct Plan and Regular Plan. This is for the exact same scheme.
  • Will I pay capital gains? Work out if switching will cause you to pay capital gain.
  • Will I pay an exit load? Check what the exit load is for your scheme and how long you’ve held your units.
  • Am I getting value for money? Do you currently get any useful support from your distributor?
  • Is this the right scheme for me? Make sure the scheme and asset allocation suits your financial goals.

If you have a large portfolio or complex tax situation you may want to speak to a qualified tax professional or appropriately registered investment adviser.

Things to check before investing

Make sure:

  • You’re investing in the correct plan type.
  • You’re investing in the correct scheme. Don’t invest in two similar schemes.
  • Compare the expense ratios. Check the latest Total Expense Ratio (TER) for your scheme.
  • Understand the risk. Read through the scheme information and understand what the risk level is.
  • Consider your goals. Make sure the fund suits your time frame and asset allocation.
  • Know who’s advising you. Do you get any services from your distributor? Are you getting registered investment advice? Or just access to transactions?
  • Keep a record. Keep a copy of your confirmation and periodically check your consolidated portfolio statement.

What does this mean for the Mutual Fund industry in India?

This puts more of a focus on showing the costs of your investment clearly. Having a default option can impact what you choose, especially if you’re new to investing in Mutual Funds and didn’t know there were two options. This means people who want to invest without using a distributor may not accidentally choose an option with a higher cost. It may also put more focus on asking your distributor what services they provide and how they charge.

However, just because it’s easier to access doesn’t mean you’ll understand how to invest. You will still need to understand the risks, diversification, costs, time frames and difference between execution and personal advice. Distributors may need to show the value they provide and AMCs should ensure they’re providing clear disclosures.

FAQs

  1. Are Regular Mutual Fund Plans no longer available from November 2026?
    No. They’re still available. However, Direct Mutual Fund Plans will now be the default option on AMCs’ digital platforms. You’ll need to be made aware of the higher expense ratios if you choose to invest in Regular Mutual Fund Plans.

  2. Will my current Regular plan automatically be switched to a Direct plan?
    No. You won’t be automatically switched. Take a look at your current holdings and consider the tax and exit load implications.

  3. Do Direct and Regular Plans invest in different stocks?
    No. Both the Direct and Regular options will have the same underlying portfolio and fund manager. The main difference is how they’re distributed and the expense ratios.

  4. Is a Direct Plan suitable for everyone?
    Not necessarily. It may be suitable for those who can pick and monitor their funds. However, if you need regular support you may appreciate the support from your distributor. Just make sure you understand the cost.

  5. Where can I find the expense ratio for a Mutual Fund?
    Check the scheme disclosures from the AMC. Also check the Total Expense Ratio information from AMFI. Compare the Direct and Regular options for the same scheme. Check the latest disclosure.

Conclusion

The change to having Direct Mutual Fund Plans as the default option is a reminder that costs are important. From 1st November 2026 you’re more likely to see the Direct Plans as the default option if you’re investing on an AMCs’ digital platforms. However, Regular Plans are still available with a higher expense ratio disclosure.

Don’t just switch or invest because it’s the default option. Make sure you understand the costs, what support you’re getting, what the risk is in the fund and if you can manage your investment. An appropriate investment decision is one that suits your financial goals and behaviours.

SIP vs Lump Sum: What Beginners Should Understand
Understand SIP and lump-sum mutual-fund investing in India through an illustrative comparison of timing risk, cash flow, discipline and market uncertainty.

A Systematic Investment Plan and Lump Sum are similar, however the main difference is the method in which you invest. A Systematic Investment Plan will invest your money into your chosen scheme by making scheduled regular contributions. With a Lump Sum you invest a larger amount of money at once (subject to processing and scheme rules). Neither name of the investment will tell you if the scheme you are investing into is suitable and both options do not guarantee that you will profit.

This question often comes up when you have some bonus money, maturity money, inheritance or savings to invest. Perhaps you want to invest some money now but are worried that the market will drop shortly, or maybe you only have a small amount of money to invest each salary. You should consider where the money is coming from and why you are looking to invest now.

## How they work

With a Systematic Investment Plan you are investing a set amount into your chosen scheme on a regular basis. You will buy units at the relevant NAV on each day your investment goes through. You will be investing the same amount each time, however depending on the NAV, you will receive a different amount of units. The schedule can help to avoid having to decide each month, however this will depend on your bank and scheme rules.

With a Lump Sum you will invest the larger amount of money you have available. If the scheme performs well then you will benefit from the increase as it will be invested as a whole. On the flip side, if the scheme performs poorly you will lose the whole amount invested. You can see when you have invested the money. You may want to invest your money in a Lump Sum to avoid having unused money, however this depends on market performance and the asset you are investing into.

## Timing Risk vs Investment Risk

Timing Risk relates to your chosen point of investment. Investment Risk relates to the assets within the scheme not performing as expected or losing value. Although a Systematic Investment Plan spreads your investment over different times, there is still a risk of holding onto an asset that is losing value. A Lump Sum will expose you to more risk at the beginning. However if prices are rising over the period you may get better returns as you have invested as a whole.

There is no reliable way to know if prices will rise or fall straight after a particular date. Trying to find the perfect time to invest can turn into a guessing game. You may also have no money left in your household if you invest all your money at once. A correct analysis should take into consideration how liquid your money is, how far ahead you are looking and what you are investing for.

## Example

Let’s look at an example with ₹60,000. One option would be to invest the whole amount at the beginning. The other option would be to invest ₹10,000 each month for 6 months. Let’s say that the unit price changes over this period (this is not actual market data and will not predict future performances).

If the prices are rising then the Lump Sum investor will have more money invested at the beginning of the period. The Systematic Investor will invest some of their cash later therefore some units will be bought at a higher price. This means that the Lump Sum may have a higher value at the end. If the prices fall at the beginning and then rise, the Systematic Investor will buy more units at the lower price. The Lump Sum will lose value at the beginning. Depending on the exact prices and when they occur, the Systematic may come out on top or the other way round. If the prices are falling and stay low then both investors could lose money. Simply spreading the investments won’t help if the investment is consistently poor.

To fairly compare you need to ensure you are investing into the same scheme, with the same end date. All of the money should be invested into the scheme, with any relevant costs. The Systematic Investment Plan will have some cash outside of the scheme. You also need to consider that the final percentage may be misleading as you aren’t comparing equal amounts.

## Benefits of Systematic Investment Plans

If you are a salaried individual then investing regularly can mirror the income you receive each month. You may not have much cash to invest so using a Systematic Investment Plan can help keep things simple. You may feel less pressured to invest at a particular date as you will be investing regularly. You can also review your investment if your income or essential costs change, as long as you stick to your scheme and mandate rules.

Although this can help keep things simple, this doesn’t mean it is the right option. If you are investing into a scheme with more volatility than you can handle then it is a risky investment. Automated payments can also continue even if your original reason for investing has changed without reviewing. Just like with a one off investment, you should research the product.

## Benefits of Lump Sums

A Lump Sum may be the best option for a one off investment such as a matured deposit. You should have already considered taxation, debt, short term costs and emergency savings. You will invest all your money at once meaning you are achieving the desired split. It can also be easier to track.

However the downside to investing at one point is that you are exposed to more risk. If the price drops suddenly you may not be happy with this, especially if you weren’t expecting the market to be volatile in the short term. You shouldn’t invest using a Lump Sum because you think the market will rise now that you have the money. If you need the money in a short period of time then it may not be suitable to invest into something linked to the market, whether it is a Lump Sum or multiple investments.

## Cash & Time Horizon

If you have money to pay for rent, medical, upcoming education or a house deposit soon then this shouldn’t be seen as spare cash to invest. Firstly you should know how much of this money is actually available to invest into something linked to the market and when you need it. If you are making regular investments into a SIP then there is an opportunity cost as you are holding onto the cash. This should be considered when comparing.

If you have a long time horizon then you will have more time to ride the volatility. However this doesn’t guarantee that it will recover by your chosen date. The market, scheme and mix of assets will still play a part. If you have a short time horizon then it becomes more important to avoid being forced to sell after a drop. Whatever method you use won’t make up for a mismatch in asset and goal.

## Common Mistakes

Assuming that SIPs are always better because they average the price. This isn’t true. Assuming that Lump Sums are always better because the money is invested for longer. This doesn’t take into consideration the timing risk and how much loss you can tolerate. Comparing a real SIP with a hypothetical Lump Sum (with a different start date) or picking a good time period.

Using past data can show you what has happened over a certain period of time. However this doesn’t tell you which will be better going forward. Charts online may not take into consideration taxation, timing of transactions, cash held between investments or the emotional impact of holding onto your investment after a drop. You should be upfront with your assumptions.

## Questions to Consider

Where is the money coming from? Monthly income or lump sum? Will it be used for a known expense? Do you have any savings available for unexpected events? What are you investing for? How far ahead are you looking? Do you understand the scheme you are investing into? Would you be forced to withdraw or change your plan if there was a sharp drop?

Your answer may vary depending on how the money is split. For example your monthly salary may not need to be invested the same as your bonus which you are saving for your goal. This is a general planning consideration.

## Conclusion

Systematic Investment Plans and Lump Sums are simply two ways to invest money into a mutual fund. A Systematic Investment Plan will spread your investments over different dates and can be a good option for regular income. A Lump Sum will invest your available cash straight away and you will be exposed to more timing risk. The outcome will depend on market performance, timing of your investment, scheme and how much cash you need. A careful comparison should be made with clear assumptions and knowing that both can lose value.

## Investing from Salary

If you are investing from your monthly salary then you may not have the cash available to invest at the beginning. Comparing a monthly SIP investment with a Lump Sum 12 months worth of salary will not be fair as you haven’t actually received the money yet. A fair comparison should be made between available cash now and money expected. This is often a more important consideration than debating abstractly about timing.

If you do have the money available then you need to decide if you want to invest it all now or spread it. By holding some cash aside you are creating a different cash allocation. This should be considered when analysing. You should consider what you are investing for and any constraints you have, rather than using a simplified chart.

## Limitations of Historical Data

You can run a back test to see how each would perform over a historical period. However this will depend on the dates you choose to start and end, scheme, timing of transactions, costs and how you are dealing with the cash. Choosing to start just before a sharp drop may favour the spread investments. Choosing a period with a prolonged rise may favour the Lump Sum. Although these are real historical examples, they won’t tell you what will happen next.

If this data is shown in an article then you should state what period you are looking at and how you have analysed it. A short period may not be representative of a long term goal. The more detailed a chart looks, the more important it is to state what isn’t included.

Term Insurance Explained: Cover, Claim Settlement Data, Riders, and Exclusions
Learn how sum assured, underwriting, disclosures, riders, exclusions and claim-settlement data should be understood without treating statistics as guarantees.

This is a life insurance product. You will receive a benefit if you pass away within the term of the policy. Often this will be referred to using the term sum assured. However, this may be detailed in the policy. This is not an investment product therefore should not be directly compared to others using the premium.

## Understanding Cover

Within your policy, the term sum assured will be an important part. However, it will not represent what your family will actually need. Depending on your circumstances, such as any financial commitments (home loan, running costs, education costs, dependents), your savings, other cover and future earnings, this can impact how much cover you may need. This article will not tell you how much cover you should have but will explain why the figure given in the headline should be understood in the context of your circumstances.

## Term

You may have a term policy. This will mean that your cover will last for a set period of time. As your children grow older, debts reduce and you have more savings you may see a change in how much cover you need. If your policy lapses whilst you still have financial dependence then you may not have enough cover. Your schedule should detail when your cover begins and ends plus the premium required.

## Underwriting

The insurer will want you to provide some information. This can include your age, medical history, occupation, lifestyle factors and any existing cover. Medicals and additional information may be requested. The insurer will decide whether to accept, decline, charge, exclude or add other terms.

Make sure that all your proposal forms are filled in correctly. Don’t miss out any information even if it seems irrelevant or someone says it will give you a better quote. Keep a copy of your application form and any declarations. If your agent/intermediary has filled in the forms for you, make sure you have read through all the answers. This could affect your claim.

## Riders

These are additional benefits added to your policy. These can be a range of things from additional benefits if you pass away due to an accident, disablement or suffer from a particular illness. The names and benefits of riders can vary so it is important to understand what they are. This can be done by reading the wording in the policy. An additional premium may be charged. To qualify for the rider there may be conditions, exclusions and a separate claims process.

Don’t assume that everything relating to the name of the rider will be covered. The definition, medical proof, time frames and exclusions will all affect this. Try to obtain a written explanation of how your rider works. Is it an additional benefit? An accelerated benefit? Does it lapse before your main cover? [CONFIRM BEFORE PUBLISHING: What is the definition of this rider? What are the current IRDAI requirements?]

## Exclusions

These are situations where you will not receive the benefit within your policy. The wording will vary depending on your policy. Don’t make general statements like "All claims will be covered from...". This should only be stated if your policy and law allows you to. Read through the exclusions, conditions, definitions and documents required.

You should also understand what happens in terms of grace periods, lapses, revival and nominations. If you don’t pay your premium correctly then your policy may lapse. Make sure that your family have easy access to the insurers details and policy number. Beneficiaries may struggle to find the documents.

## Understanding Claims Data

There is lots of data available from insurers and regulators. The most popular being the claims ratio. This can be misleading as it depends what is in the denominator, how long the time frame is, what types of claims are included, if it is based on amount or numbers and if it includes pending claims. Always look at what the exact definition is in the official report.

A high ratio doesn’t mean that your claim will be accepted. A lower ratio doesn’t mean that your claim was not paid. This will depend on your policy, any disclosures, medical proof, exclusions and whether the claims process was followed. Claims data should be used as a general background only.

Don’t use the number from the article, make sure you have the source, time frame and what it is measuring. [CONFIRM BEFORE PUBLISHING: What is the latest claims data from IRDAI? What is the time frame? What is the definition? Any caveats?] If this isn’t present in the official report don’t guess.

## Beneficiaries and Claims

Nominations can help you understand who your beneficiary is. This will depend on the law and policy. The policyholder should ensure the details are correct. They should also update the details after a major life event. Don’t rely on nominations to understand the legal ownership and succession. Complex families may need advice.

Keep your schedule, proposal, premium receipts and correspondence with your insurer together in a place your family can easily find. Let them know where to look but don’t share any sensitive information. Your beneficiaries should know how to formally make a claim with the insurer, and what documents are generally required. The current claims process should be followed.

## Affordability

Whilst you have cover this will only be beneficial. If you lose your job, your income changes or your family have more commitments then this can become a burden. Before signing make sure that you can afford to pay for the premium. This shouldn’t affect your ability to pay for your home, debts, health etc. Check the dates and what payment options are available in the official terms.

Don’t cancel your existing cover without thinking. New cover may need to go through underwriting and won’t be on the same terms. If there are any changes make sure you understand when the new contract will begin and what happens to the old contract.

## Queries

What is the benefit? How long will my cover last? What is the premium? What will I need to declare? Are there any exclusions? Can I update my nominee details? How will claims work? Ensure you have the full wording of any riders. If there is a difference between what has been said in the sales information and in the policy ask the insurer to provide a written explanation.

## Conclusion

Term insurance relies on clear terms, correct disclosures and following the policy. Read through the sum assured, term, riders and exclusions. Claims data can only be used as a background and you should understand what it means and the time frame. It won’t tell you if your claim will be successful. Use current IRDAI information and official policy documents. This is a general explanation and should not be taken as a personal recommendation.

## Free Look/Grievance

Depending on the regulations your policy may have a free look/review period. Check what the conditions and time frames are in the current regulations and policy. As soon as you receive the policy read through it. Ensure that this is what you applied for. If there is a material difference between what has been explained and the actual policy contact your insurer formally.

Keep a note of your complaint number, any written communication and final response. IRDAI provide official information for policyholders. The process and timeframes can vary, link to current guidance. Never say that a claim will be guaranteed to have a specific outcome from a regulator.

## Sales Illustration Wording

Words such as guaranteed, projected, bonus and illustrated can all mean different things. Ask the insurer to highlight what is a contractual obligation and what will be declared in the future. Don’t rely on the colour of the chart. Keep a copy of your illustration.

## Claims File

The policy owner may not be the one making the claims. Keep your schedule, proposal, premium receipts, nomination details and insurer details together. A simple note of where they can be found will save time. Keep your file safe as it will contain personal and financial information. Ensure that the correct family member can find it.

Depending on your insurer and regulations you may be asked to provide ID, proof of death and other documents. This will vary. Use the current official claims checklist from your insurer. If there is a delay in claiming keep a note of the reference number and ask for the missing requirement in writing.

## Data

If there is a ratio at insurer level in the publication ensure you can locate the table. You should be able to replicate the definition. Policies or amounts? What is the time frame? There are many terms within health insurance that can cause confusion when trying to understand what has been paid for your hospital bill. Wait periods, co-payments and sub-limits are three key terms that often get confused with each other. However, each term has its own purpose. Wait periods are there to limit cover for a specified period of time or condition. Co-payments allow you to claim a percentage of a claim that falls within the policy. Sub-limits are there to limit the pay-out for a specific cost or treatment. As these can be used in conjunction with one another, it is best to read the whole schedule to see what benefits you have.

## Wait Periods

Many health insurance policies will have an initial wait period. The length of this will vary between policies, however, it will state what happens during the initial waiting period. Depending on the policy, it may state that any claims made within the initial wait period will be handled differently.

The initial wait period should not be confused with the start date. A policy can be in place but still have limited claims. If you are taking out insurance close to when you want to have a procedure, just because you have a policy doesn’t mean you can claim for any medical costs.

## Specific Disease/Procedure Wait Periods

Within your policy there may be a list of specific diseases, treatments or procedures that will only be covered from the date stated. There will be a variety of things listed and how they are described. This may not be fully covered by the wording in the brochure, please refer to the policy wording and customer information sheet. If your diagnosis has many names or complications relating to it, please ask your insurer for clarification.

These can affect decisions, but shouldn’t be used as an excuse to not receive medical treatment. If you need medical treatment you shouldn’t put it off due to a general explanation. Please ask your insurer to clarify what is covered within your policy. The medical professionals will decide what treatment you should receive.

## Pre-existing Disease

Pre-existing disease refers to conditions set out in the policy and regulations. Please ensure you know what conditions are included, how long the look back period is and how long the wait period is. This will be set out within the policy. When applying please be honest with your medical history. If you have a condition that is managed by medication it can still be relevant to the application. Don’t assume it’s not relevant just because you don’t think it is.

[Please verify current IRDAI wording on pre-existing and specific disease maximum wait periods within the health insurance regulations.] If there are any changes to the rules please update this article with the official notification and the date it comes in to effect.

## Co-payment

Co-payment means that you will pay a specific percentage or proportion of the claimable costs. A deductible may be included in the policy that will mean you have to pay a set amount before the policy will pay. The co-payment can be a percentage of the whole claimable costs or may only apply to certain situations. Please refer to the exact wording within the policy.

For example, if you had a hospital bill with £80,000 of claimable costs and the policy had a 10% co-payment this would equate to £8,000. You would then have £72,000 of claimable costs. This is not an accurate calculation as there may be some items that aren’t claimable or have a limit. This is just an example.

## Room Rent Limit

A room rent limit will limit what room you can stay in or how much you can claim. This may be a limit on how much you can claim in rupees, a percentage of the sum insured or something else. If the policy states that other hospital costs are linked to the room you are allowed to stay in, you may find that choosing a more expensive room affects more than the room cost. Please refer to the policy wording to see how this is calculated. Not all insurers will have the same proportional deduction.

Before being admitted to hospital please ask what would happen if you are offered a room outside of the allowed room? What would be reduced and by how much? This may depend on the policy, hospital charges and how the insurer sees it. Just because the hospital can guarantee you a room doesn’t mean you will be able to claim for the room.

## Sub-limits & Exclusions

A sub-limit means there is a maximum amount you can claim for a specific cost or treatment. An exclusion means that you may not be able to claim for the item at all. Both can be present in the policy. Please check the summary to see what applies.

Check what specific procedures, ambulance, consumables, non-medical items and outpatient treatments are included. The policy will vary. Are there any limits? Is it per claim, per year, per procedure or is there another condition? The name will not tell you how it interacts with other clauses.

## Example

Say you have a hospital bill of £150,000 (this is purely an example). £20,000 of the items are excluded. You now have £130,000 to consider. There may be a sub-limit on a specific procedure. There may also be a room rent clause. There may then be a 10% co-payment applied to the remaining claimable amount. The insurer will have calculated this based on the policy wording. You will not be able to replicate what they have done as each clause will need applying in the order set out in the policy.

This example shows that just because a policy states they will cover £5lakh it does not mean they will pay the full £1.5lakh. The sum insured is just part of the policy. To calculate a real claim you would need to look at the policy schedule, wording, hospital invoices and what the insurer has decided.

## How to compare the terms

Within the policy schedule and customer information sheet please note down what the initial wait period, specific disease wait periods, pre-existing condition clause, co-payment, deductible, room eligibility, sub-limits and exclusions are. Compare like for like. A lower premium may have cost sharing or less limits. There is no one factor that will give you the full value of the policy.

Don’t assume everything is covered. Please ask for the clause and note this down. If the insurer is not clear please ask them for clarification via their official customer channel. The policy wording and current regulations should help.

## Common Misconceptions

A wait period does not mean the whole policy isn’t in place. A co-payment isn’t the same as a deductible. A room rent limit may affect other costs if the policy states it. Having a high sum insured won’t remove exclusions or sub-limits. It is good to understand these differences ahead of any hospital event as you may not have time to read through them all in detail due to the stress.

## Conclusion

Wait periods, co-payments and sub-limits are all separate features that can affect your claim. How they affect you will depend on the exact wording and current regulations. Use examples to understand how they work numerically. The policy schedule, official IRDAI information and asking for clarification in writing will help.

If you haven’t received as much as you were expecting please ask for a breakdown of the calculations. Please ask what clause was used for each deduction. Split up the exclusions, co-payment, deductible, room adjustment and any sub-limits. These aren’t interchangeable terms and may all affect the same bill. Having this in writing will help you see where the difference is.

If you are still unsure please use the insurer’s formal complaints process. Keep copies of your bill, claim form, pre-authorisation request, settlement statement and any correspondence. Refer to the current IRDAI information on policyholder complaints to ensure you escalate correctly. We cannot decide whether a real claim should be paid based on this article. You need to refer to the contract and facts.

Whenever an insurer issues an endorsement or renewal please save it with the original policy wording. If you just save a summary, it may not reflect the new wording. If you have multiple policies within your family please label them with the name of the insured, dates and insurer. This will help avoid using incorrect wording when making a claim.

Ask the insurer what the start date is, when each waiting period ends and whether the condition is a pre-existing, specific or excluded condition. Ask what the reference to the clause is within the policy wording. If you only receive a verbal answer please ask for clarification via their official customer channel. If you can get a clear answer before you take out the policy it will be easier to understand.

When comparing two contracts please write down the details. Don’t just assume a policy has a short waiting period or no room limit. Check what exclusions, co-payments and any other limitations there are. The current regulations and wording will determine what the situation really is. Please check the wording again if the policy is renewed or changed.

Term Insurance vs Savings-Type Life Insurance Plans
Compare term protection and savings-oriented life insurance, including premiums, benefits, liquidity, lock-ins, exclusions and policy questions for consumers.

Often life insurance can be viewed as one product, however there are a number of different products available. Term life insurance is typically a pure product offering life cover for a specific period of time. Savings life insurance products often include some form of life cover and a saving element which will depend on the terms of the policy. When looking at life insurance products you may have to look at the terms and conditions of each product to fully understand what they are offering.

## Purpose of the product

Life insurance is to provide the named beneficiaries with a payout if they die whilst the policy is active. The amount they receive is usually referred to as the sum assured however this will depend on the terms and conditions of the policy. The money received can be used by your family to recover lost income, pay off debts or for future costs however the amount of cover will not be determined by the contract.

Savings life insurance products may provide some benefit at maturity if the person lives up to the maturity date. This may be guaranteed, non-guaranteed or dependant on declared bonuses. It can often be wrongly assumed that all values shown in the sales illustration are guaranteed, however you should check that there are clear references to what is guaranteed within the contract.

## Cost of Premiums

The premium will depend on many factors such as underwriting, product, level of cover, length of cover, age and more. Term products tend to have lower premiums than savings life insurance products as they do not include any accumulation or maturity element. However features, terms and conditions will vary so you should not compare quotations unless they are for the same level of cover.

Just because a policy has a low premium it doesn’t mean it offers great value and vice versa. You should look at the terms and conditions to understand when you will receive a payout, what conditions apply and the impact of stopping payments. Understanding if there is a grace period, what happens if the policy lapses, what the revival terms are and if there are reduced paid up benefits can be very important.

## Liquidity

Generally speaking term insurance isn’t a saving product and you won’t get your premium back if you change your mind. If they do offer a return of premium this will be a specific feature of the contract so you should read carefully. Savings products may have a surrender or paid up clause however if you cancel your policy early you may receive a significantly different value. You should not assume your policy is a source of cash.

Ask what the surrender terms are and how the value will change. After a short period of time you may not have as much as you expect. Surrendering your policy will also mean you lose the cover. If you need your savings to be liquid you should understand the difference between the money you have saved in your insurance contract and what you can withdraw from a bank account.

## Terms and Conditions

All insurance products will have terms and conditions. These will vary between policies so you shouldn’t assume generic answers. The proposal form will also be important. Be honest and thorough when answering the questions relating to your health, smoking, occupation, existing policies and more. If you answer these incorrectly you may make claiming complicated in the future. You should keep a copy of your proposal form, medical information and correspondence with the insurer.

Look at the free look, cancellation, grace period, revival and intimation terms. Check what the current regulations are by referring to IRDAI and the official terms. [CONFIRM: current regulations regarding disclosure, free look period, grace periods and claims for the policy you are describing.]

## Guaranteed vs Assumed values

If it’s a savings product ask the insurer what is guaranteed and what is assumed. Look at when the premium will be paid, when the benefits will be paid, what happens if they die during different years of the policy, what the maturity terms are, what happens if you surrender and what happens to the bonuses. The maturity value shown will be a single value so you should look at when you’ll receive and what the terms are.

If it’s a term product understand what happens if they die, how long the term is, when the premium will be paid, if there are renewal or conversion terms, and if the payout is a lump sum. Riders may affect the terms and cost. Don’t just look at the single line premium.

## Tax implications

Depending on the type of policy, premium, date of issue, terms and conditions and the tax regime, tax implications can vary. Don’t assume all premiums are deductible and all maturities are tax free. [CONFIRM: current tax implications for the relevant life insurance contract under the Income-tax Act, 2025 for Tax Year 2026-27.]

Don’t enter into a long term contract purely because of the tax benefits. Tax rules can change and you will need to consider the cost, liquidity and benefits. Refer to official documentation from the Income Tax Department and seek professional advice from a qualified tax professional.

## Key Questions

What triggers the payout, who will receive it, how long will you be paying the premium, what happens if you miss a premium, what is guaranteed, how much will you receive if you surrender early, are there any exclusions or waiting periods, how will you make a claim and what documents may you need? This information should be available in official documentation.

You should also consider if you can afford to pay the premium if you change jobs, become ill or have family expenses. If you can no longer afford to pay your policy may lapse. If you have a long term policy you should consider doing a realistic cashflow to see if you can afford it. If you have other major goals within your family this should be considered.

## Common Misconceptions

Term insurance is not a liquid investment. Savings insurance is not the same as a bank account or mutual fund. The maturity value may not be guaranteed and can include assumed values. Tax implications will vary between policies and tax payers. You should understand the product based on the terms.

## Summary

There are often big differences between term and savings life insurance products. Look at the actual contract, guaranteed values, non-guaranteed values, surrender terms, exclusions and premium commitment. Confirm the current tax and regulatory terms from official sources. This will help you understand the features of the product. It does not recommend any particular policy or how much cover your family will need.

## Nomination and Family Communication

It can be difficult to manage insurance within your family if no-one knows about your policy or where the documents are kept. Keep a personal record of which insurers you have, policy numbers, when you need to pay and where your policy is. Let the right family member know how to find the information without revealing any sensitive data. Review your nomination details if you get married, separated, have a baby, pass away or have another major change within your family.

The legal implications of having a nominee can vary depending on the situation and law. Don’t assume that having a nominee will solve any issues with inheritance or ownership. If you have a complex family structure it may be appropriate to seek professional legal advice. You should still read the policy to understand how to make a claim and what documents may be required.

## Can I afford it?

Consider if you can afford to pay the premium if your income drops temporarily or you have another major expense. As this is a long term product you shouldn’t just consider the initial premium. If you miss a payment it will depend on the grace, lapse and revival terms of your policy. Read these terms in advance and ask for written clarification if they are unclear.

## Changing Circumstances

Your life rarely remains the same throughout the term of your insurance. You may take out a new loan, have a child, change jobs or take care of a parent. Consider if you still want the same level of cover and premium commitment. However you should read the terms of your policy. Cancelling your policy could leave you without cover and you may have to take out a new policy which may involve new underwriting.

Ask your insurer what changes can be made to your policy, can the sum assured be changed and what are the terms for converting, paid up or surrendering. Don’t assume that what your agent tells you verbally will be a benefit in your contract. Keep written confirmation and compare to your policy. The purpose of reviewing is to understand your options and what will happen.

What Is a SIP? How Monthly Investing Works in India
Learn how SIPs work in India, including mutual-fund units, NAV, instalments, rupee-cost averaging, missed payments and investment risks for beginners.

A systematic investment plan (SIP) simply refers to investing a pre-determined sum into a mutual fund scheme at regular intervals. Due to salaries and household budgets often being in monthly chunks many investors opt to invest each month. It is simply an investment method and not an investment asset or guarantee. The money will be invested into whichever scheme you have chosen and will be subject to the value of the underlying scheme.

SIPs can help create structure but do not eliminate market risk. It is important to consider the underlying scheme, its value, what you will be charged and whether you might need the money soon. While it can create structure in your investing by having fixed amounts taken out of your account, it will not help you invest in a scheme that doesn’t suit your needs. Mutual funds are linked to the market (unless specified otherwise due to the scheme structure and holdings), meaning the amount returned could be less than what you have invested.

Let’s say you have instructed your platform or mutual fund provider to take ₹2,000 (example amount) from your account each month. When the payment is successful you will be buying units in the scheme you have selected based on the scheme rules and NAV. You will not receive a fixed number of units each month. The amount of units you receive will depend on the amount invested and the applicable NAV, whilst considering any charges that apply.

The Net Asset Value (NAV) shows the value of a mutual fund scheme’s assets after liabilities have been accounted for. This is then divided by the number of units in the scheme. This is generally published each business day. However just because you see a scheme with a lower NAV of ₹20 compared to ₹40 does not mean it is cheaper or better. This is because the schemes may have different assets, history and risk. It is similar to seeing two receipt totals in a shop.

If you invest ₹2,000 (example amount) and the NAV is ₹25 you will receive 80 units. If you decide to invest another ₹2,000 and the NAV has dropped to ₹20 you will receive 100 units. If the NAV has increased to ₹40 you will receive 50 units. This will vary depending on the scheme rules and documentation.

## Rupee Cost Averaging

Investing fixed amounts regularly will mean at lower NAVs you will get more units and vice versa. This is known as Rupee Cost Averaging. However it does not guarantee you’ll make a profit. If the scheme falls in value over a period of time you may still end up with less value in your units.

Let’s say you invest ₹1,000 (example amount) each month. The NAVs are ₹10, ₹20 and ₹25. This means you would have bought 190 units (100+50+40) for a total investment of ₹3,000. Your average cost per unit is around ₹15.79. If the NAV drops to ₹12 your total investment would be worth ₹2,280 (before any charges or tax). Just because the average cost is lower than some of the purchase prices doesn’t mean you will make a loss.

## SIPs are not an investment

Sometimes people talk about investing in a SIP. A SIP is actually simply an investment method. The scheme is what you are investing in. Even if you have an equity, debt or hybrid scheme they can all have very different risks. Having a monthly contribution does not change the objective, the portfolio or the risk of losing value.

Before investing in a scheme always read through the scheme information document, key information memorandum and risk statements. Consider the scheme’s objective, portfolio, benchmark, charges, redemption rules and level of risk. Don’t just invest because your friend is investing, it looks good on social media or has had a great return recently. Past performance is historical data and cannot be relied upon.

## Amount and timing

Consider all of your monthly outgoings such as rent, food, transport, family support, EMIs, insurance and irregular payments. Whilst you may think you can afford the monthly contribution, you may find it stressful when you have to pay for school fees, repairs or travel. It’s generally better to have a sustainable amount.

The timing of your SIP can be important. Some people choose to have it after they have received their salary. Others may want to have a buffer in place as the timing of your salary, bank holidays and standing orders may not line up perfectly. Try to ensure you have enough in your linked bank account for any essential payments. You shouldn’t miss out on paying an EMI for your loan, have a bounced payment for utilities or have to use expensive revolving credit due to your SIP.

## Missed Payment

If your bank payment hasn’t gone through it generally means you won’t be purchasing the scheme as instructed. Depending on the provider, bank mandate, platform and scheme rules this will vary. If there are repeated issues the SIP may be cancelled based on the applicable rules. There may also be charges from your bank/intermediary. Be sure to read through your mandate and service carefully.

Just because you haven’t invested in this month it doesn’t mean you’ve lost all your units. They will still be invested unless they’ve been redeemed. However it could affect your goal based investing as less money has been invested. If you’re experiencing a cash flow issue it’s best to review your instructions and household budget.

## Risks

The market can fall, interest rates can fluctuate, there is a risk of default and the scheme portfolio may not perform as expected. Equity schemes can be volatile in the short term. Debt schemes also have risks such as credit and interest rate risk. Hybrid schemes combine risks but will still have the potential to lose value. Understanding the risks of the fund isn’t as simple as looking at the name.

There is also practical risks. You may stop investing during a falling market and start again when prices have risen. You may not choose a scheme that suits the timing of when you need the money. Someone may think the example calculator gives a guaranteed result. Your plan should allow for uncertainty.

## Common misconceptions

A SIP does not guarantee you’ll make a profit. It doesn’t guarantee you’ll have a lower average cost than lump sum investing. It doesn’t guarantee that equity schemes are safe in the short term. Whilst it’s automated from your bank it doesn’t mean the scheme has been considered for your situation. You still need to understand the product.

The NAV isn’t a rating. Just because it’s lower doesn’t mean it has more scope to increase. Just because it’s higher doesn’t mean it’s expensive. The portfolio, charges, investment strategy and risks are much more important than the unit price.

## Practical review

Ensure you keep a copy of your scheme documentation and transaction confirmation. Just to make sure the correct amount was invested into the correct scheme. Understand how to pause, amend or cancel your instructions. Don’t get too caught up with the daily fluctuations. Instead look at how you’re doing with your goals and how the scheme fits with the objective stated. It’s also a good idea to check whether your goal date, income or household commitments have changed.

For a first time investor the most valuable thing to understand is the difference between your bank balance, units in your mutual funds and the fluctuating market value. Once you understand this you will find it easier to understand how useful a SIP can be.

## Conclusion

A SIP can help create a regular investing habit. Every time you successfully invest you will be buying units based on the applicable NAV. This will mean the number of units will vary depending on the price. This is known as Rupee Cost Averaging. However you need to consider the underlying scheme, the risks, your time frame and whether your household can sustain investing. Always refer to official investor education and scheme documentation. This article is purely explaining how it works and won’t help you find a scheme suitable for you.

## Reviewing your transactions

After investing ensure you have a copy of your transaction confirmation. Ensure that the units have been added to your account. If the money has gone out of your bank but it doesn’t look like you’ve invested, check the transaction date, units issued date and applicable NAV. Mutual funds have cut off and settlement rules so the NAV and date may not match exactly. Speak to your provider and check the official transaction history.

It’s also useful to understand the difference between what you have invested and what it’s currently worth. You may see the total invested, units held and current value. The current value will fluctuate depending on the NAV. The original investment amount is historical data. This doesn’t necessarily mean there has been an issue. If the figures don’t match review your transaction history and scheme documentation.

## How often to review

Checking your mutual fund balance multiple times a day can create a sense of a personal crisis due to normal market fluctuations. Setting a review date based on your goals can be more useful. Confirm your transactions, check how the scheme fits with its objective and ensure you can still afford to invest. If there has been a significant change to your income, goal date or household commitments you may want to review sooner. A drop in NAV won’t necessarily mean it no longer fits with your original purpose.

Refer to official investor education and scheme documentation to better understand the risks. Remember all projections are scenarios and any market related balances will fluctuate.
